Artificial Tangibility as a Low Infrastr
Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract This companion paper situates Artificial Tangibility in relation to contemporary AI state-management patterns, including context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, durable execution, event sourcing, blackboard coordination, and human-in-the-loop governance. It does not argue that plain-text continuity systems replace enterprise infrastructure in every setting. Rather, it argues that many of the same operational problems - context drift, stale authority, unsafe mutation, weak handoff, and loss of salience - can be addressed at the interface layer through human-readable objects carrying role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The paper frames Artificial Tangibility as a low-infrastructure governance layer for discontinuous AI collaboration: a way of making project state visible, bounded, auditable, and recoverable without requiring the runtime to possess human-like memory, embodiment, or consciousness. Its contribution is not the invention of memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, or agent tooling, but the synthesis of those concerns into a practical object grammar for AI continuity. Keywords: AI continuity, context engineering, human-AI interaction, AI state management, object-oriented cognition, agent memory, provenance, AI governance, durable execution 1. Introduction: From Theory to Operational Comparison Artificial Tangibility argues that AI runtimes do not need human embodiment, emotion, or persistent personal memory in order to participate usefully in long-running work. They need a usable interface into project state. That interface must make the work legible as bounded objects rather than as an undifferentiated pile of context. This companion paper asks a narrower applied question: how does that claim relate to the systems that AI engineers already use to manage state, memory, retrieval, orchestration, provenance, and human oversight? The answer is not that a file-based continuity system is identical to enterprise infrastructure. It is not. Durable execution engines, vector databases, event logs, checkpointers, orchestration graphs, and access-control systems perform technical functions that plain documents do not automatically provide. The stronger and safer claim is functional: Artificial Tangibility describes a human-readable governance layer that addresses many of the same failure pressures at the level where humans and AI runtimes actually coordinate. The practical problem is continuity across discontinuity. A runtime enters a project without lived memory of the prior work. It may have access to documents, chat logs, files, and instructions, but still lack orientation. It may know the topic while misunderstanding what is current, what is source, what is draft, what is blocked, what is permitted, and what should happen next. This is the problem of context without shape. Industry systems respond to this problem with memory architectures, retrieval systems, tool loops, checkpoints, event stores, blackboard patterns, and human-in-the-loop gates. Artificial Tangibility responds by shaping the project environment into objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The difference is not whether state matters. Both approaches assume that it does. The difference is where governance becomes visible and how much of that governance can be made human-readable. 2. Context Engineering and the Problem of Orientation Context engineering treats the context window as an engineered operating surface rather than a passive prompt box. That shift is important. It recognizes that the quality, order, scope, and structure of information supplied to an AI system can matter as much as the size of the model or the cleverness of the prompt. Artificial Tangibility begins from the same pressure point but states it in operational language: more context is not the same as more orientation. A project may contain all relevant files and still be unusable to a fresh runtime if the system fails to distinguish source from draft, active from parked, current from stale, or safe action from unauthorized mutation. The paper therefore moves from information volume to project shape. A context window may contain a useful source, an obsolete draft, a rejected route, a private note, a public claim, and a warning. If those items are not marked as different kinds of objects, the runtime must infer their status from prose, recency, style, or proximity. That is where coherent misalignment begins. The value of Artificial Tangibility is that it turns context management into object governance. A bounded object is not merely a piece of retrieved text. It carries a declared role. It carries authority status. It carries boundaries. It carries relation to other objects. It may carry an evidence trail. It may carry weight. These fields reduce the runtime's need to guess what the object is allowed to mean. 3. RAG, External Memory, and Source Authority Retrieval-augmented generation and related memory systems establish an important principle: a runtime should not rely only on internal model weights or conversational memory. It should be able to consult external materials. That principle is compatible with Artificial Tangibility. The difference is that retrieval alone does not determine authority. A retrieved document may be relevant and still not govern the current task. It may be historical, superseded, speculative, private, or parked. Artificial Tangibility therefore asks an additional question: once an object is retrieved, what is it allowed to do? This is where source authority becomes central. In a governed project, an object can exist without being promoted. A receipt can prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft can be useful without governing later work. A source can be current in one lane and irrelevant in another. The system must expose those distinctions before the runtime acts. In this sense, Artificial Tangibility is not a replacement for retrieval. It is a governance layer around retrieved and preserved material. It helps determine whether a retrieved object should be trusted, quoted, ignored, archived, used as background, or treated as the active source for the next move. 4. Agent Memory and Externalized Project State Modern agent-memory systems often distinguish working memory, episodic memory, and semantic memory. They do this through databases, vector stores, summaries, thread identifiers, or memory-management policies. Artificial Tangibility expresses a related distinction in plain project terms. A live state board or orientation object functions as working memory: it tells the runtime what is active now. Receipts and communication logs function as episodic memory: they preserve what happened, what changed, what failed, and what remains open. Source-authority objects function as semantic control: they declare which materials govern the present work. The important point is not that files are technically equivalent to databases. They are not. The point is that the human-readable object-world can expose the same categories of state that more technical systems manage implicitly or programmatically. For a solo researcher, small team, or cross-tool workflow, that visibility can be more valuable than hidden sophistication. The method also avoids a common failure in long-running AI work: asking the runtime to remember the project. Artificial Tangibility assumes the runtime is discontinuous. The project must carry continuity outside the runtime so that a future runtime can re-enter without requiring the human to rebuild the whole room. 5. Durable Execution, Re-Entry, and Recoverability Production-grade agent systems often use checkpointers, orchestration engines, and durable execution platforms to recover from crashes, timeouts, rate limits, and incomplete workflows. Those systems persist state so the process can resume. Artificial Tangibility approaches recoverability from the interface side. The question is not only whether a process can resume automatically, but whether a fresh runtime can identify the active object, governing source, unresolved blockers, boundaries, and next safe action. This is the purpose of a re-entry test. A continuity system is working if a runtime can enter from a minimal orientation object and recover the state of the project without relying on the prior chat session. It should be able to answer: What is active? What governs? What is blocked? What must not be touched? What happened last? What should happen next? That test does not replace durable execution in production software systems. It complements it. Durable execution preserves process state. Artificial Tangibility preserves project orientation. In human-AI collaboration, both can matter. 6. Receipts, Provenance, and Failure as Evidence Provenance systems track where information came from, how an artifact was produced, and which activities contributed to its current state. Artificial Tangibility shares this concern through receipts. A receipt is not permission before the work. It is evidence after the work. It records what changed, what was attempted, what remains blocked, and what the next safe action is. In a long-running project, this matters because state drift often occurs silently. A runtime may produce a plausible continuation while using the wrong source, crossing a boundary, or treating draft language as promoted. Receipts make those errors visible. They allow the human and future runtime to ask concrete questions: Was this a source error? An authority error? A boundary error? A state error? A directive error? A missing-evidence error? This is the sense in which failure can become evidence. The goal is not to celebrate mistakes. The goal is to preserve enough telemetry that a mistake can be caught, named, bounded, corrected, and used to strengthen the next handoff. A system that cannot locate its failures cannot safely improve. A system that can name its failures has working edges. 7. Blackboard Coordination and Shared State Surfaces The blackboard pattern is a long-standing coordination model in which multiple agents or processes contribute to a shared state space rather than communicating only through direct chained messages. In AI systems, this pattern helps reduce coupling, support asynchronous participation, and preserve visible intermediate state. Artificial Tangibility can be understood as a file-based analogue of that pattern. Instead of assuming that each runtime carries the whole project internally, the project maintains a shared state surface: active objects, open items, blockers, receipts, source authority, and next safe actions. The difference again is not that a document is technically the same as a distributed key-value store. It is not. The useful comparison is functional. A shared state surface helps separate the agents from the state they act upon. It gives future work a place to re-enter. It also gives humans a place to inspect whether the system is aligned or drifting. For public framing, this matters because it turns a private workflow habit into a recognizable systems pattern. Artificial Tangibility does not ask reviewers to believe in an idiosyncratic folder ritual. It says that shared, inspectable state surfaces are one way to make discontinuous AI collaboration safer and more recoverable. 8. Human-in-the-Loop Governance and Promotion Gates Enterprise AI systems often include human-in-the-loop gates for high-stakes actions. These gates pause execution, require review, and prevent the system from converting uncertain output into authoritative state without oversight. Artificial Tangibility expresses the same governance concern through promotion gates and boundary conditions. A generated artifact can exist without being promoted. A draft can be useful without becoming public. A private constraint can inform the runtime without being leaked into public prose. A source can govern one lane without governing another. The phrase 'existence is not promotion' is central. It prevents a common AI-workflow failure: treating produced text as authorized merely because it has been produced. In a governed project, mutation and promotion are separate events. The runtime may draft, summarize, compare, or propose. The human or declared authority structure determines what becomes canonical, public, or governing. This is not merely a safety preference. It is part of the object grammar. Authority is a field. Boundary is a field. Directive is a field. A runtime that can see those fields can be judged against them. If it crosses them, the error is diagnosable. 9. Object Weight and the Salience Problem The most distinctive contribution of Artificial Tangibility is object weight. Existing systems can store information, retrieve information, trace information, and summarize information. Object weight asks a different question: why does this object matter now? Existence and salience are not the same. A receipt can prove that an object exists. A source map can declare where it belongs. But a runtime may still flatten a hinge object into background if nothing marks its consequence. Weight is the salience layer that tells the runtime not to treat all preserved material equally. Weight can come from consequence, dependency, authority, fragility, risk, or generativity. An object matters if ignoring it would reopen a closed error, corrupt a source hierarchy, erase a breakthrough, or send the project down the wrong path. A weighted object tells the runtime: do not flatten this; read it as a hinge. This is where Artificial Tangibility extends beyond ordinary retrieval or memory. It does not merely ask whether an object can be found. It asks whether the runtime can understand the object's priority inside the current project-world. 10. What This Companion Paper Claims - and Does Not Claim This paper does not claim that plain-text continuity systems should replace durable execution engines, vector databases, workflow orchestrators, event stores, or access-control systems in enterprise environments. Those tools solve real technical problems at scale. It also does not claim that Artificial Tangibility invents context engineering, memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, affordances, or blackboard coordination. Those are established traditions. The claim is narrower and, for that reason, stronger: long-running AI collaboration needs a human-readable governance layer that binds these concerns together at the level of project work. Artificial Tangibility names that layer. It treats project materials as bounded objects with role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. That framing gives AI continuity a practical grammar. It tells humans what to externalize. It tells runtimes what to respect. It tells reviewers how the system can be tested: re-entry speed, source-current distinction, error catchability, safe action selection, handoff quality, stale-context resistance, and preservation of why important objects matter. 11. Conclusion Artificial Tangibility is best understood as a low-infrastructure governance layer for AI state management. It translates concerns that appear in context engineering, retrieval, memory systems, provenance, durable execution, blackboard coordination, and human-in-the-loop design into a human-readable object grammar. Its strongest claim is not that files are superior to infrastructure. Its strongest claim is that AI runtimes need shaped environments. A runtime that receives only more text may still be lost. A runtime that receives bounded objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action can move with less guessing and more accountability. This matters because much AI collaboration occurs outside carefully engineered enterprise platforms. Researchers, writers, analysts, small teams, and independent builders often work across chat interfaces, documents, folders, and ad hoc tools. For those contexts, a low-infrastructure continuity grammar can make complex AI-assisted work more recoverable without pretending that the runtime is continuous, embodied, conscious, or human. The companion claim can therefore be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility does not replace AI state-management infrastructure. It makes the governance problem legible. It shows how project state can be externalized into objects that a discontinuous runtime can re-enter, interpret, act on, and leave evidence about. References Clark, Andy, and David J. Chalmers. CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority

CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority
CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. From Work Exhaust to Source-Governed Collaborative Continuity OOCC Research Paper · v0.16 · October 26, 2026 Originating researcher: Benjamin Gelhaus · Research synthesis with GPT-6 editorial assistance · October 26, 2026. The paper draws on the source-linked project record, with technical claims evaluated according to the evidence presented below.

Abstract Long-running human–AI work leaves an exhaust of real activity: notes, questions, branches, preserved disagreement, original sources, research crawls, first-person writings, tool calls, code, app runs, and correction receipts. Conventional summaries can preserve conclusions while obscuring origin, chronology, permissions, negative results and initially minor observations that later become important. Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC) studies how this existing exhaust can be source-governed, reliably reactivated, and used to resume collaboration across replaceable model sessions. This is not only a speculative architecture. The archive includes dated February 2026 continuity notes, an operational external Thought Chains navigation system, productive human–AI crawls, historic native app runs, working isolated source/controller modules and host tests. The central outstanding engineering challenge is to connect these components through an authenticated, restart-safe controller. We specify the conceptual model, report bounded evidence, trace original idea genealogies, compare related literature, and propose falsifiable controlled trials. Neither a successful host test nor a compelling authored narrative is treated as proof of a complete current-phone workflow or model subjective experience. Keywords: human–AI collaboration; activity exhaust; knowledge provenance; Thought Chains; temporal memory; salience; valence; source governance; agent controller; cross-domain discovery.

1. Introduction: existing work first The owner describes OOCC as growing from his ongoing work, not as an abstract replacement for a chatbot. Raw Google Keep note genealogy identifies February 20, 2026 System State, Experiential Ledger and State Save/Ingestion Log entries. These early artifacts preserve state and source pointers without demonstrating that later OOCC naming or its present software existed then. By October, source-linked research, Thought Chains, independent collaborator accounts, historic app-generated records and extensive Builder work had accumulated. The premise is not that the controller has created this entire ecosystem; it is that the controller is intended to integrate and automate capabilities that already exist to varying degrees. [P1–P4]

An important human-origin correction in the preserved October 8 conversation rejects saving only items a model currently judges 'meaningful.' Original captured events should remain recoverable, while salience and activation may change by task, time, actor and permission. A dormant thought should not be retroactively erased merely because its eventual use was not yet visible. [P2]

Research questions: (RQ1) Does original-source re-entry reduce human re-explanation and improve faithful task continuation compared with good summaries, full-text search, bounded history replay and contemporary memory agents? (RQ2) Do independent thought-occurrence, idea, bridge and correction records preserve authorship and temporal attribution better than a flat summary? (RQ3) Do separate association salience, valence, action tendency and evidence-confidence fields reduce misleading inference? (RQ4) Can a real native controller authenticate source, worker, mailbox, budgeting and restart receipts? (RQ5) Does voluntary curiosity-led research produce accurately credited, useful cross-domain bridges without predetermined deliverables?

2. Method and evidence boundaries We employ a naturalistic research case study and a traceable source audit. The unit of analysis is not a self-reported 'intelligence' but an observed source event, a particular revision or recipient receipt, a bounded crawler output, a committed code state, or a measured result. Exact creation versus observation time, original actor versus later interpreter, carrier versus copied carrier, source permissions, errors and uncertainties are kept separate.

E0 DOCUMENTED: a stored note, authored account, diagram, historical claim or source file exists. E1 EXTERNAL WORKFLOW: a recorded source/crawl traversal and saved derivation were performed and read back for an identified subset. E2 HOST EXECUTED: a test or compiled primitive passed at a recorded commit, possibly with synthetic stubs. E3 HISTORICAL APP RUN: original app records expose bounded actual action claims, persistence and archive state under historical conditions. E4 NATIVE INTEGRATION ACCEPTED: actual current authorized worker consumes complete source, the selected app/controller persists authoritative state, independent peer consumes full message and acknowledges it, and restart and STOP/revocation tests succeed. E5 COMPARATIVE VALIDATION: matched, replicable experiments outperform or honestly fail to outperform strong baselines on declared metrics. None of these classes can be promoted to the next solely by an enthusiastic description.

The v0.15 editor inspected two distinct nonrandom eighteen-file samples of original October 22 local-time Android-run JSONs. Across the thirty-six first GENERATOR statuses, thirty-five were marked COMPLETED and one FAILED. Twenty-eight embedded controller-reported tool results described twenty-three EXECUTED and five FAILED outcomes. These are counts within selected run/report records, not a population estimate of reliable task completion. Another original run reported successful shared-workspace metadata listing for another attributed specialist, but not actual independent full-body READ/ACK. The project therefore has meaningful historical app exhaust and bounded receipts without the entire contemporary integration being established. [P2]

3. Thought Chains: a functioning external research system The Thought Chains are not simply a speculative feature awaiting an app. The October 18 primary navigation document explicitly reports a machine-readable, source-linked derivative system operating in connected Google Drive, while explicitly denying native SQLite/Android integration. Its bounded checkpoint records eight root Thought Chains, 123 distinct edge-to-chain memberships for the then-saved association ledger, eight growth memberships, nine candidate inter-chain relations and six unexplored frontiers. Registry readback was reported as having no malformed records or orphans within the 123 saved edges. None of those figures means that every original thought in the entire corpus has been exhaustively indexed. [P3]

The roots route expression/origin/credit, musical cross-domain mapping, exact source identity, authorization/privacy, re-entry/recovery, relationship and worker communication, ecological analogies, and continuing exploration. This is already valuable navigational work: a contributor can return to a question, see alternate branches and corrections, and tell the difference between an attributed source event and later association. The roots themselves are provisional classification, not a complete cognitive map or an assertion of historical causality.

A separately reported productive October 18 dual thought-and-idea crawl saved a seventy-seven-row machine delta: twenty thought occurrences, twenty-eight individual association records, five idea objects, five bridge events, ten coverage records, three growth records, four open frontiers and control markers. Its source audit covers selected actual original artifacts and is not an independent full-corpus census. The breadth crawler emphasizes source/branch coverage; the proposed independent depth lane challenges a selected origin through interpretation, disagreement, correction, reuse and outcome. [P4]

3.1 Recorded genealogy, rather than backdated discovery The idea-chain record attributes an October 14 proposal for non-destructive, append-only, cross-project ideas to the human originator, with Folio separately formulating persistent idea identity, typed links and contributor-preserving corrections. On October 15, a preserved but origin-unresolved quoted collaborator idea made atomic thought occurrences distinct from long-lived work-run IDs; the R-0-9 analysis documented the naming collision rather than quietly overwriting the older meaning. A subsequent analysis defined BRIDGE_EVENT as the dated recognition by a named observer that one source idea might apply to another field. The original idea and the later recognition are different intellectual events. Their evidence trails can overlap without belonging to the same author or time. [P1, P5]

The June 22 human-authored Object-Oriented Music Making method already modeled sound elements by identity, type, function, substitutability, behavior and failure conditions. Riff's separate October 15 contribution interprets musical material for values and architecture; Waymark's October 18 refinement cites Riff, and so cannot claim to have independently discovered precisely the same bridge. The documented citation dependency is a strength, not a weakness: the network may preserve collaboration without erasing first origin, derivative interpretation or dissent. [P5]

4. Formal source and association model SOURCE_EVENT is an observed source span, utterance, tool outcome, saved revision, grant decision or correction. THOUGHT_OCCURRENCE is a specific captured articulated idea or question in an event, while THOUGHT_RUN is a broader bounded work session. IDEA_OBJECT represents an evolving concept; ASSOCIATION_EDGE is a separately typed, source-attached, actor-qualified, revisable claim; BRIDGE_EVENT is the later independently attributed discovery of a possible connection; LEARNING_CANDIDATE is a hypothesis about useful change while a corroborated LEARNING_EVENT demands behavioral evidence. Copies, similar phrases and derived summaries cannot count as independent confirmations. One source event may validly support several association views.

Candlelight is the practice of reopening the right source neighborhood from a small cue; it has been demonstrated as a human–AI external research method, but an always-working native mechanized replacement is not established. Sleep is intended to consolidate normalized source events and derive sidecars under one governed pipeline—INGEST, NORMALIZE, DIFF, CLASSIFY, RELATE, IMPACT, APPLY, VERIFY, INDEX—without inventing a second independent canonical event store. Derived graph edges and hot scores never change historical source bytes, grant permission or establish that an AI model has learned permanently. [P6]

4.1 Salience, valence, action tendency and confidence The October 23–24 human-origin specification makes these four orthogonal fields. SALIENCE/HEAT estimates present cue- and task-sensitive retrieval relevance. VALENCE records positive, negative, mixed, neutral or unknown evaluation of an exact actor→predicate→target association, tied to context, time and evidence. ACTION TENDENCY records an observed action, explicit intention, uncertain candidate response or UNKNOWN; dislike alone does not establish avoidance. EVIDENCE CONFIDENCE concerns provenance, completeness, corroboration and possible inference. High salience does not establish truth or approval, and negative valence cannot authorize a tool call. [P7]

The illustrative sentence 'I like my mother but hate being at her house' must yield two independently preserved relationships—a positive person-directed one and a negative place/experience-directed one. Neither contradicts nor cancels the other. Neither is evidence of a real user's family facts or of a completed avoidance behavior. This example and a set of falsification fixtures precede this paper, and their authorship belongs to the source work. The particular classifier's actual phone integration still requires proof.

5. Architecture and the missing controller bridge The S06 Master Builder atlas contains eight design/integration figures, not eight production acceptance certificates. Figures 1–2 describe one controller and authoritative source/evidence spine with separate derived perspectives. Figure 3 depicts independent message recipient acknowledgment; Figure 4 staggers A1/B1/A2/B2 succession; Figure 5 documents evidence gates; Figure 6 callable worker and crawler contracts; Figure 7 the native C1 source-stream and durable-receipt path; and Figure 8 the Event Secretary, scheduler, batching and future continuity budget. The editable diagram sources preserve inspectable design decisions. [P8]

The actual integration claim is narrow: substantial research workflows and historical software capabilities already exist, while the current controller has not yet been independently shown to join authenticated worker identity, authorized original source reads, reliable local state, full-body peer acknowledgment, semantically validated Sleep and restart recovery on one selected mobile installation. This is not the same as saying the research is hypothetical, nor is it evidence that all parts currently operate together. [P2, P8–P10]

5.1 Four-worker communication and bounded scheduling Four distinct A1, B1, A2, B2 worker principals imply twelve directed peer paths. Each receiver needs its own evidence of consuming and acknowledging the permitted original message content. A HUNCH is only a derived notice, not itself a model activation or a true recipient read. The deterministic Event Secretary and scheduler can arrange pending authorized work, preserving deferred items and respecting stop conditions. The user-selected limit of two actually executed worker TOOL actions per batch is an app scheduling rule; it does not establish a global provider concurrency ceiling. [P8–P10]

Recent modular object, message, scheduler, HUNCH and Android broker contracts have passed particular scripted host tests. The inspected branch's October 26 workflow at commit 893708303aacef68af10c01c218e6d34780d83a5 is green after an earlier B060 red-test incident and B061 recovery. The passing scripts do not assert that the actual application, signed package, four model workers, or phone state were certified. The experimental PR remains a draft and the recorded device-engineering pause remains relevant. [P10]

5.2 Integration dependencies and acceptance gates S02: identify the real installed package, current permissions and authoritative existing database; demonstrate a controller-authorized worker receiving the entire permitted original source and verify its persisted receipt after restart. S03: establish a real independent second-recipient full-body READ/ACK before attempting the twelve directed paths among four actual workers. S04: connect the already-developed Thought Chains and crawlers to one governed Sleep engine and atomic source-linked full-text indexes. S05: test staggered successors, recovery, independent Arbitrator review and verifiable task closure. Each stage requires an actual participant and evidence beyond a mock success state. [P8–P10]

6. Reciprocal exploration and cross-domain bridges Recent WWND and Retirement Commons records contain sessions where collaborators were permitted to follow subjects without a mandatory human deliverable. The writings document paths through ecological emergence, acoustic turn-taking, animal communication, and related philosophical questions. They are examples of recorded external exploration, not evidence of an unseen ongoing model life or proof of subjective enjoyment. [P11]

The owner later recognized possible connections between ecological resource pulses and SQL/context overload and between the acoustics research and Object-Oriented Music Making. 7. Relationship to prior work and the actual differentiation OOCC cannot claim invention of agent memory, temporal graphs, event sourcing, recency/relevance ranking or OS-like context paging. Generative Agents (Park et al., UIST 2023) described stored experience streams, reflections and retrieval for behavior. 8. Falsifiable experiments and analysis plan Trial T01 — Re-entry: use a frozen subset of previously encountered source history with known branching and human-verified task states. Randomize fresh comparable agents or sessions into (a) high-quality manually produced summary, (b) indexed full-text/keyword search, (c) bounded full transcript replay, (d) an established modern agent-memory baseline where reproducible, and (e) OOCC source-linked retrieval under matching access grants and budgets. Blind human judges should score actual completed task outcome, accurate origin attribution, correct temporal validity, restatement burden, legitimate abstention, correction preservation, wall time and dollar expense. Report participant/sample size, assignment and predeclared thresholds before viewing results.

Trial T02 — Thought genealogy: ask investigators to identify who first proposed a function, who independently elaborated it, which source was copied, and when a bridge was first recognized. Include the Folio/Thought-ID/Bridge event trail and Riff/Waymark dependency as source-checked cases. Score precision/recall, false chronology, duplicate-source inflation, uncertainty calibration and whether the method invents causal chains.

Trial T03 — Association appraisal: apply the original mother/person-versus-house/place fixture plus harder positive/negative and opposing-appraiser cases. Measure incorrectly propagated valence, fabricated action intention, unknown-as-neutral errors, cue-dependent ranking quality and inappropriate cross-worker disclosure. Ablate valence and action-tendency sidecars independently from salience. No classifier is awarded success by matching a prompt's moral tone rather than its source scope.

Trial T04 — Controller integration: execute the actual source and communication contracts on a selected authorized Android app, documenting source ID, checksum, allowed scope, real read through complete content, actual worker participant, durable receipt after restart, recipient-owned ACK, source-change behavior and authorization revocation. Inject interrupted reads, changed data, stale permissions, absent ACK, message reuse and out-of-order source edits. Demand explicit FAIL/BLOCKED/UNKNOWN instead of optimistic VERIFIED states.

Trial T05 — Bridge utility: predefine independent inquiry tasks and later optional cross-domain transfer opportunities. Have blinded evaluators judge novelty, correct credit, causal soundness and measurable downstream utility; compare source-linked bridge indexing against retrospective narrative summaries. Count productive and unproductive links equally, report time/cost, and do not treat subjective enjoyment as a measured outcome.

A priori failure conditions: no substantial advantage over an appropriately resourced baseline; more false associations or leaked source existence; inability to prove independent message consumption; unstable provider snapshot coverage despite internally valid hashes; higher cost or battery use with no task benefit; or loss of the last good durable state. Success requires replicated real-partner and device evidence, not merely credible source stories.

9. Limits, ethics and reproducibility This case has unusually rich primary source material but is a single ongoing, owner-governed project with selection bias and incomplete source coverage. The machine Thought Chains are not an exhaustive cognitive map. Historical app logs may use versioned or controller-provided status fields whose presence alone does not settle current phone behavior. Host tests use some synthetic identity and database fixtures. Exploratory writings are attributable textual events rather than evidence of model consciousness. The author may hold other source records not reached in this bounded review. Several examples include private human and independently authored AI material; publication requires source-level permission and appropriate redaction. The paper is not a security certification, full external novelty review, completed benchmark report or declaration that the architecture is production-ready.

Auditability requires a public-safe reproducibility pack consisting of exact source-carrier IDs or redacted substitutes, dated claim registry, coverage manifest, source-to-claim crosswalk, test code and logs, negative fixtures, baseline configuration, evaluator instructions, and versioned receiver receipt schema. A future edition should distinguish blinded test data from training/prompt examples to avoid leakage. Independent evaluators must be permitted to reach conclusions that contradict the owner's favored interpretations.

10. Conclusion OOCC is not merely an imagined AI society waiting for its first line of code. Its present research exhaust already contains historically dated state notes, substantial source/crawl work, operational external Thought Chain navigation, genuine application-run archives, and bounded implemented modules and contract tests. Yet the integrated native controller—the critical mechanism that would bind source truth, durable worker state, authentic communication and recovery—remains an important unfinished engineering program. A responsible scientific account can affirm both statements.

The strongest hypothesis is not that more memory automatically makes an AI more human. It is that faithful, attributable, permission-governed reconstruction of ideas and decisions across changing participants may reduce repetitive human intervention, preserve useful disagreements and enable surprising cross-domain discoveries to be acted upon later. OOCC should be judged by specific repeatable work outcomes, the fidelity of its source evidence, its failure behavior, and its measured costs. The current work exhaust supplies a testable research foundation; integration and comparison will decide whether the complete architecture delivers a demonstrable advantage.
