From Work Exhaust to Source-Governed Collaborative Continuity OOCC Research Paper · v0.16 · October 26, 2026 Originating researcher: Benjamin Gelhaus · Research synthesis with GPT-6 editorial assistance · October 26, 2026. The paper draws on the source-linked project record, with technical claims evaluated according to the evidence presented below.
Abstract Long-running human–AI work leaves an exhaust of real activity: notes, questions, branches, preserved disagreement, original sources, research crawls, first-person writings, tool calls, code, app runs, and correction receipts. Conventional summaries can preserve conclusions while obscuring origin, chronology, permissions, negative results and initially minor observations that later become important. Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC) studies how this existing exhaust can be source-governed, reliably reactivated, and used to resume collaboration across replaceable model sessions. This is not only a speculative architecture. The archive includes dated February 2026 continuity notes, an operational external Thought Chains navigation system, productive human–AI crawls, historic native app runs, working isolated source/controller modules and host tests. The central outstanding engineering challenge is to connect these components through an authenticated, restart-safe controller. We specify the conceptual model, report bounded evidence, trace original idea genealogies, compare related literature, and propose falsifiable controlled trials. Neither a successful host test nor a compelling authored narrative is treated as proof of a complete current-phone workflow or model subjective experience. Keywords: human–AI collaboration; activity exhaust; knowledge provenance; Thought Chains; temporal memory; salience; valence; source governance; agent controller; cross-domain discovery.
1. Introduction: existing work first The owner describes OOCC as growing from his ongoing work, not as an abstract replacement for a chatbot. Raw Google Keep note genealogy identifies February 20, 2026 System State, Experiential Ledger and State Save/Ingestion Log entries. These early artifacts preserve state and source pointers without demonstrating that later OOCC naming or its present software existed then. By October, source-linked research, Thought Chains, independent collaborator accounts, historic app-generated records and extensive Builder work had accumulated. The premise is not that the controller has created this entire ecosystem; it is that the controller is intended to integrate and automate capabilities that already exist to varying degrees. [P1–P4]
An important human-origin correction in the preserved October 8 conversation rejects saving only items a model currently judges 'meaningful.' Original captured events should remain recoverable, while salience and activation may change by task, time, actor and permission. A dormant thought should not be retroactively erased merely because its eventual use was not yet visible. [P2]
Research questions: (RQ1) Does original-source re-entry reduce human re-explanation and improve faithful task continuation compared with good summaries, full-text search, bounded history replay and contemporary memory agents? (RQ2) Do independent thought-occurrence, idea, bridge and correction records preserve authorship and temporal attribution better than a flat summary? (RQ3) Do separate association salience, valence, action tendency and evidence-confidence fields reduce misleading inference? (RQ4) Can a real native controller authenticate source, worker, mailbox, budgeting and restart receipts? (RQ5) Does voluntary curiosity-led research produce accurately credited, useful cross-domain bridges without predetermined deliverables?
2. Method and evidence boundaries We employ a naturalistic research case study and a traceable source audit. The unit of analysis is not a self-reported 'intelligence' but an observed source event, a particular revision or recipient receipt, a bounded crawler output, a committed code state, or a measured result. Exact creation versus observation time, original actor versus later interpreter, carrier versus copied carrier, source permissions, errors and uncertainties are kept separate.
E0 DOCUMENTED: a stored note, authored account, diagram, historical claim or source file exists. E1 EXTERNAL WORKFLOW: a recorded source/crawl traversal and saved derivation were performed and read back for an identified subset. E2 HOST EXECUTED: a test or compiled primitive passed at a recorded commit, possibly with synthetic stubs. E3 HISTORICAL APP RUN: original app records expose bounded actual action claims, persistence and archive state under historical conditions. E4 NATIVE INTEGRATION ACCEPTED: actual current authorized worker consumes complete source, the selected app/controller persists authoritative state, independent peer consumes full message and acknowledges it, and restart and STOP/revocation tests succeed. E5 COMPARATIVE VALIDATION: matched, replicable experiments outperform or honestly fail to outperform strong baselines on declared metrics. None of these classes can be promoted to the next solely by an enthusiastic description.
The v0.15 editor inspected two distinct nonrandom eighteen-file samples of original October 22 local-time Android-run JSONs. Across the thirty-six first GENERATOR statuses, thirty-five were marked COMPLETED and one FAILED. Twenty-eight embedded controller-reported tool results described twenty-three EXECUTED and five FAILED outcomes. These are counts within selected run/report records, not a population estimate of reliable task completion. Another original run reported successful shared-workspace metadata listing for another attributed specialist, but not actual independent full-body READ/ACK. The project therefore has meaningful historical app exhaust and bounded receipts without the entire contemporary integration being established. [P2]
3. Thought Chains: a functioning external research system The Thought Chains are not simply a speculative feature awaiting an app. The October 18 primary navigation document explicitly reports a machine-readable, source-linked derivative system operating in connected Google Drive, while explicitly denying native SQLite/Android integration. Its bounded checkpoint records eight root Thought Chains, 123 distinct edge-to-chain memberships for the then-saved association ledger, eight growth memberships, nine candidate inter-chain relations and six unexplored frontiers. Registry readback was reported as having no malformed records or orphans within the 123 saved edges. None of those figures means that every original thought in the entire corpus has been exhaustively indexed. [P3]
The roots route expression/origin/credit, musical cross-domain mapping, exact source identity, authorization/privacy, re-entry/recovery, relationship and worker communication, ecological analogies, and continuing exploration. This is already valuable navigational work: a contributor can return to a question, see alternate branches and corrections, and tell the difference between an attributed source event and later association. The roots themselves are provisional classification, not a complete cognitive map or an assertion of historical causality.
A separately reported productive October 18 dual thought-and-idea crawl saved a seventy-seven-row machine delta: twenty thought occurrences, twenty-eight individual association records, five idea objects, five bridge events, ten coverage records, three growth records, four open frontiers and control markers. Its source audit covers selected actual original artifacts and is not an independent full-corpus census. The breadth crawler emphasizes source/branch coverage; the proposed independent depth lane challenges a selected origin through interpretation, disagreement, correction, reuse and outcome. [P4]

The June 22 human-authored Object-Oriented Music Making method already modeled sound elements by identity, type, function, substitutability, behavior and failure conditions. Riff's separate October 15 contribution interprets musical material for values and architecture; Waymark's October 18 refinement cites Riff, and so cannot claim to have independently discovered precisely the same bridge. The documented citation dependency is a strength, not a weakness: the network may preserve collaboration without erasing first origin, derivative interpretation or dissent. [P5]
4. Formal source and association model SOURCE_EVENT is an observed source span, utterance, tool outcome, saved revision, grant decision or correction. THOUGHT_OCCURRENCE is a specific captured articulated idea or question in an event, while THOUGHT_RUN is a broader bounded work session. IDEA_OBJECT represents an evolving concept; ASSOCIATION_EDGE is a separately typed, source-attached, actor-qualified, revisable claim; BRIDGE_EVENT is the later independently attributed discovery of a possible connection; LEARNING_CANDIDATE is a hypothesis about useful change while a corroborated LEARNING_EVENT demands behavioral evidence. The editable diagram sources preserve inspectable design decisions. [P8]

This is not the same as saying the research is hypothetical, nor is it evidence that all parts currently operate together. [P2, P8–P10]

Each receiver needs its own evidence of consuming and acknowledging the permitted original message content. A HUNCH is only a derived notice, not itself a model activation or a true recipient read. The deterministic Event Secretary and scheduler can arrange pending authorized work, preserving deferred items and respecting stop conditions. The user-selected limit of two actually executed worker TOOL actions per batch is an app scheduling rule; it does not establish a global provider concurrency ceiling. [P8–P10]
Recent modular object, message, scheduler, HUNCH and Android broker contracts have passed particular scripted host tests. The inspected branch's October 26 workflow at commit 893708303aacef68af10c01c218e6d34780d83a5 is green after an earlier B060 red-test incident and B061 recovery. The passing scripts do not assert that the actual application, signed package, four model workers, or phone state were certified. The experimental PR remains a draft and the recorded device-engineering pause remains relevant. [P10]

S04: connect the already-developed Thought Chains and crawlers to one governed Sleep engine and atomic source-linked full-text indexes. S05: test staggered successors, recovery, independent Arbitrator review and verifiable task closure. Each stage requires an actual participant and evidence beyond a mock success state. [P8–P10]

Use an unassisted baseline where ethical, plus matched con‐ ventional notes and modern agent memory. With consenting additional volunteers, compare across reported attention/ex‐ ecutive-function needs without claiming clinical status from system logs. Keep consent, privacy and accessibility reviews separate. Actual grant eligibility, open competitions, participant protections and institutional requirements need verification at the time of application. The earlier dated research claims keep their original evidence classifications. ===================================== ======================= Research Addendum — November 3, 2026 Low-Marginal-Cash, Multi-Track Independent Research: A Longitudinal Feasibility Case Study Status: Author-supplied longitudinal research addendum. The counts and prior veri‐ fication are reported by the supplied source account; under‐ lying originals and work-ticket records were not independ‐ ently re-audited in this PDF conversion. This is a single-re‐ searcher observational case, not a controlled experiment. Research question Can an independent researcher use ordin‐ ary consumer AI services, existing personal storage, and a source-governed continuity method to sustain substantial re‐ search and engineering activity while simultaneously man‐ 12 aging employment and other consequential responsibilities, without purchasing dedicated research infrastructure? Method and source corpus The supplied case-study record describes an original ChatGPT conversation export covering February 4 through October 21, 2026, supplemented by dated source documents, software-engineering records and contemporaneous employment-related email records. Repor‐ ted archive totals: 289 conversation graphs; 86,120 graph nodes; 15,740 user-authored message nodes; archive size 148,989,570 bytes. The reported SHA-256 fingerprint of the original archive is c53003d21266973fc00bff6741282c16de88d1f42ad7e657e‐ be262a669aabc5d. Message timestamps were converted to America/Denver and grouped by calendar date. Conversation branches were preserved instead of being treated as one uninterrupted chronology. Findings 1. Sustained longitudinal activity The source account reports user-authored activity on 161 distinct calendar days in a 260- day observation window. Activity was present in at least two distinct archived conversation titles on 95 days; at least three titles on 62 days; and at least five titles on 32 days. These are activity measures, not direct measures of productive hours, completed tasks or output quality. 2. Concurrent employment and technical work On six sampled dates—September 29 and October 8, 15, 16, 17 and 20, 2026—corresponding self-reported paid-work records total 55.25 hours. The source account also reports 1,504 user-authored message nodes dated to those six days. This establishes overlapping calendar dates, not work conducted during paid hours or measured research time. 3. Multiple substantial development tracks The reported archive and separately preserved artifacts document legal 13 and legislative analysis, original writing, evidence organiza‐ tion, AI continuity engineering, source archiving and re‐ search-method development, including OOCC and related tools. The subsequently documented V2 crawler execution re‐ ports processing 289 archived conversation graphs in a base extraction workflow, with source hashes, SQLite records, checkpoint evidence and reproducible scripts. Source-repor‐ ted local software tests must be separated from unverified native deployment and real-world effectiveness. 4. Low additional cash expenditure The researcher reports that ChatGPT and Google storage subscriptions already served personal uses; the research reused those resources. A short-term paid Claude subscription for an external runtime audit is recorded in an earlier OOCC book and should be in‐ cluded in a final research-specific expense ledger, alongside any other attributable payments. The available account sup‐ ports low incremental out-of-pocket spending for substantial documented work—not an audited claim of zero cost. Person‐ al labor, hardware, cloud-provider resources and opportunity cost must be distinguished from direct payments. Interpretation The documented case supports feasibility in one instance of substantial independent AI-assisted research and engineering using consumer-accessible tools alongside employment and other responsibilities. It does not establish that the OOCC method causally increased productivity relat‐ ive to a strong conventional workflow. Its distinctive setting involves frequent project switching and interruption-driven recovery. Limitations and next validation stage This is a single-re‐ searcher longitudinal case study. Message counts indicate activity rather than quality. ChatGPT exports do not capture all work in Google Drive, other AI systems, software reposit‐ ories or offline settings. The original archive, time-zone pro‐ cessing, work records and financial ledger must be made 14 available in a privacy-reviewed reproduction packet to estab‐ lish the reported counts independently. Next tests should measure matched deliverables, human labor hours, interrup‐ tion-recovery time, source accuracy, completed-task quality, direct expenses and full resource costs against capable conventional research workflows. Provisional conclusion Substantial source-documented inde‐ pendent research and engineering production is reported us‐ ing consumer-accessible infrastructure alongside other major responsibilities. An exact cash advantage and causal pro‐ ductivity improvement remain open to comparative measure‐ ment. CRAWL-V2-001 — Crawler Perspective and Evidence Log, October 22, 2026; checkpoint and repro‐ ducible evidence bundles. OOCC Research Book v0.16-S1, October 26, 2026; existing economics and external-runtime audit. Original employment work-ticket emails for the six sampled overlapping dates. OOCC software repository and dated GitHub Actions records retained separately from the archive period. Economic-model boundary The previously discussed $40,000–$133,000 conventional replacement-cost range re‐ mains a separately labelled scenario model, not an observed saving. That estimate is not added to observed expenditure. END OF NOVEMBER 3 RESEARCH ADDENDUM. The follow‐ ing source transcript preserves the November 2 research edi‐ tion in its original order. MEAS‐ UREMENT: Preselect real-life and controlled re-entry tasks; preserve source/time/role/outcome and the author's actual course corrections; compare time to accurate working-posi‐ 11 tion recovery, number of human clarifications, required con‐ text-reconstruction words, correct-deliverable rate, inde‐ pendently checked source fidelity, omissions and safe refusal. Use an unassisted baseline where ethical, plus matched con‐ ventional notes and modern agent memory. With consenting additional volunteers, compare across reported attention/ex‐ ecutive-function needs without claiming clinical status from system logs. Keep consent, privacy and accessibility reviews separate. FUNDING / FIELD ALIGNMENT, NOT AWARD: As‐ sistive-technology research, cognitive accessibility, digital health, and human-computer interaction are candidate re‐ search categories. Actual grant eligibility, open competitions, participant protections and institutional requirements need verification at the time of application. No government fund‐ ing, educational-device approval or FDA authorization is as‐ serted. EDITORIAL BOUNDARY: This added note supple‐ ments—but does not rewrite—the preserved 198-page source research PDF below. All following material is extracted, page by page, from that PDF. The earlier dated research claims keep their original evidence classifications. ===================================== ======================= Research Addendum — November 3, 2026 Low-Marginal-Cash, Multi-Track Independent Research: A Longitudinal Feasibility Case Study Status: Author-supplied longitudinal research addendum. The counts and prior veri‐ fication are reported by the supplied source account; under‐ lying originals and work-ticket records were not independ‐ ently re-audited in this PDF conversion. This is a single-re‐ searcher observational case, not a controlled experiment. Research question Can an independent researcher use ordin‐ ary consumer AI services, existing personal storage, and a source-governed continuity method to sustain substantial re‐ search and engineering activity while simultaneously man‐ 12 aging employment and other consequential responsibilities, without purchasing dedicated research infrastructure? Method and source corpus The supplied case-study record describes an original ChatGPT conversation export covering February 4 through October 21, 2026, supplemented by dated source documents, software-engineering records and contemporaneous employment-related email records. Repor‐ ted archive totals: 289 conversation graphs; 86,120 graph nodes; 15,740 user-authored message nodes; archive size 148,989,570 bytes. The reported SHA-256 fingerprint of the original archive is c53003d21266973fc00bff6741282c16de88d1f42ad7e657e‐ be262a669aabc5d. Message timestamps were converted to America/Denver and grouped by calendar date. Conversation branches were preserved instead of being treated as one uninterrupted chronology. Findings 1. Sustained longitudinal activity The source account reports user-authored activity on 161 distinct calendar days in a 260- day observation window. Activity was present in at least two distinct archived conversation titles on 95 days; at least three titles on 62 days; and at least five titles on 32 days. These are activity measures, not direct measures of productive hours, completed tasks or output quality. 2. Concurrent employment and technical work On six sampled dates—September 29 and October 8, 15, 16, 17 and 20, 2026—corresponding self-reported paid-work records total 55.25 hours. The source account also reports 1,504 user-authored message nodes dated to those six days. This establishes overlapping calendar dates, not work conducted during paid hours or measured research time. 3. Multiple substantial development tracks The reported archive and separately preserved artifacts document legal 13 and legislative analysis, original writing, evidence organiza‐ tion, AI continuity engineering, source archiving and re‐ search-method development, including OOCC and related tools. The subsequently documented V2 crawler execution re‐ ports processing 289 archived conversation graphs in a base extraction workflow, with source hashes, SQLite records, checkpoint evidence and reproducible scripts. Source-repor‐ ted local software tests must be separated from unverified native deployment and real-world effectiveness. 4. Low additional cash expenditure The researcher reports that ChatGPT and Google storage subscriptions already served personal uses; the research reused those resources. A short-term paid Claude subscription for an external runtime audit is recorded in an earlier OOCC book and should be in‐ cluded in a final research-specific expense ledger, alongside any other attributable payments. The available account sup‐ ports low incremental out-of-pocket spending for substantial documented work—not an audited claim of zero cost. Person‐ al labor, hardware, cloud-provider resources and opportunity cost must be distinguished from direct payments. Interpretation The documented case supports feasibility in one instance of substantial independent AI-assisted research and engineering using consumer-accessible tools alongside employment and other responsibilities. It does not establish that the OOCC method causally increased productivity relat‐ ive to a strong conventional workflow. Its distinctive setting involves frequent project switching and interruption-driven recovery. Limitations and next validation stage This is a single-re‐ searcher longitudinal case study. Message counts indicate activity rather than quality. ChatGPT exports do not capture all work in Google Drive, other AI systems, software reposit‐ ories or offline settings. The original archive, time-zone pro‐ cessing, work records and financial ledger must be made 14 available in a privacy-reviewed reproduction packet to estab‐ lish the reported counts independently. Next tests should measure matched deliverables, human labor hours, interrup‐ tion-recovery time, source accuracy, completed-task quality, direct expenses and full resource costs against capable conventional research workflows. Provisional conclusion Substantial source-documented inde‐ pendent research and engineering production is reported us‐ ing consumer-accessible infrastructure alongside other major responsibilities. An exact cash advantage and causal pro‐ ductivity improvement remain open to comparative measure‐ ment. Primary evidence references identified by the source account Original author-held ChatGPT HTML export, February 4–Oc‐ tober 21, 2026. Reported SHA-256: c53003d21266973fc00bff6741282c16de88d1f42ad7e657e‐ be262a669aabc5d. CRAWL-V2-001 — Crawler Perspective and Evidence Log, October 22, 2026; checkpoint and repro‐ ducible evidence bundles. OOCC Research Book v0.16-S1, October 26, 2026; existing economics and external-runtime audit. Original employment work-ticket emails for the six sampled overlapping dates. OOCC software repository and dated GitHub Actions records retained separately from the archive period. Economic-model boundary The previously discussed $40,000–$133,000 conventional replacement-cost range re‐ mains a separately labelled scenario model, not an observed saving. That estimate is not added to observed expenditure. END OF NOVEMBER 3 RESEARCH ADDENDUM. The follow‐ ing source transcript preserves the November 2 research edi‐ tion in its original order. BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL | GELHAUS 2026 The most practical path forward preserves the existing source-authority machinery and introduces targeted extensions: precise refusal diagnostics, exact-field source routing, event candidates distinct from their documentary appearances, versioned correction relationships, and optional evidence-gated relation exploration. Those extensions admit concrete tests and provide McPhetridge with incremental opportunities to improve coverage without compromising the safeguards that already work. The OOCC development record supplies a related methodological lesson. V3 succeeded V2 through a documented history of tests, negative findings, and implementation changes. An external critique of one version must be dated and tested against that version’s actual evidence; conclusions cannot be inherited unchanged after revisions. Applying the same standards of chronology, source identity, and measurable outcome to both architectures turns comparative criticism into an engineering instrument rather than a contest of presentation or assertion. Host-test outcomes separately scoped in the original audit. [O6] OOCC V2 A10 ten original graph checkpoints and V2 B8 ten bounded source-depth checkpoints , 6–7 November 2026. Historical V2-family contract invocations; V2 does not remain the current crawler architecture. Reports distinguish full export topology from sampled semantic readings and report unsupported historical claims as unresolved; private original custody preserved. [R1] Comparative Evaluation Error Audit , 14 November 2026. Private research-session record of source-order, chronology, and evidence-weighting errors; hypotheses about causal mechanisms are catalogued separately. Describes CRAWL-V3 as the successor crawler, records distinct A/B lanes and source/checkpoint routing, and explicitly labels native controller operation, recipient acceptance and unattended execution as unverified. This is a working-state candidate, not the sole governing OOCC orientation. Private source custody retained; original ID withheld from public supplement. Appendix A. Acceptance tests for proposed extensions The acceptance suite should pin code revision, configuration, source bytes, field normalization, external-model settings and computational budgets before each run. Hidden questions must remain separate from development examples. BENJAMIN GELHAUS · 14 NOVEMBER 2026 | 15 BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL | GELHAUS 2026 1. No regression in source authority. Existing integrity, supersession, restricted-source, conflict and negative controls must retain their answer support and refusal decisions. 2. Improved diagnostic truthfulness. Unsupported question grammar, absent eligible source, known source conflict, insufficient evidence and index-exhaustion must be separately labeled. 3. Exact identifiers without false pruning. Exact field/quote routing must improve source location in held-out cases without dropping contradictory eligible passages; test zero, one and multiple matches. 4. Distinct event identities. Multiple appearances of one message remain distinguishable source occurrences; equal subject lines must not force identity; changed bodies must trigger review. 5. Time-scoped correction. A later partial correction changes only its specified claim while retaining the original statement, provenance and prior assessment. 6. Candidate inference remains a candidate. Missing intermediate evidence stops the proposed relation; exploratory outputs do not appear as deterministic supported answers. 7. Operational receipts remain independent. Stored, dispatched, delivered, read, acknowledged and completed are distinct outcomes; every transition requires the designated evidence. 8. Measure operator burden. Report human labeling and correction time, CPU time, memory, bytes scanned, source-count coverage and false-bridge rates alongside top-k retrieval. The decisive falsifier of the present capability-gap claim is an identifiable, independently examined MPLPB implementation that reconstructs these relationships from unprepared original source records , with credible source citations, useful recall, low false-positive rates and no degradation of its existing authority protections. A reciprocal evaluation of OOCC should use the same original-source access, version pins, blinded scoring and error metrics, while also measuring workflow benefits not shared by the two intended designs. An early critical claim about OOCC is falsified only by evidence attached to the correct date and technical mechanism, not by an unrelated later success. BENJAMIN GELHAUS

candidates.body_html:
CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority

CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Free public author editions Benjamin Gelhaus offers free downloadable research books and practical methods at https://independent.academia.edu/ BenG197. Check the publication date and edition number: other author- posted copies may be earlier working editions. The book’s “Activate PDF” instruction is inside the text, not printed as a command on the cover. In this EPUB the original print-source page divisions are tracked through unobtrusive internal identifiers for comparis‐ on with the PDF. Tables are represented as source-order text where necessary. Reading order: the original cover is first. The regular reading edition places the complete Activate PDF procedure and han‐ doff test in the final appendix, after the source exhibits. The historical print-source table of contents retains its original page numbers; use this EPUB’s linked Contents for naviga‐ tion. 2 About this November 2026 edition No More First Dates With AI — Regular reading edition. Written by Benjamin Gelhaus, with separately attributed as‐ sistance from GPT-6 collaborators where stated. This is a re‐ vised reading and distribution format of a historically sourced OOCC corpus. The November 6 publication lineage and its original contributor records are preserved. November 9 additions are dated editorial contributions; their presence does not retroactively change the original event record. What the cost claim means Agent-like results describes observed multi-session, human- directed work using ordinary ChatGPT tools, Google Drive, explicit roles and source-verified checkpoints. It does not mean zero cost, unlimited usage, independent always-on agents, or no human intervention. The evidence does not in‐ clude a controlled total-cost comparison with commercial agent products. Actual plans, storage, subscription limits and tool access can change. candidates.body_html:
Artificial Tangibility as a Low Infrastr

Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract This companion paper situates Artificial Tangibility in relation to contemporary AI state-management patterns, including context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, durable execution, event sourcing, blackboard coordination, and human-in-the-loop governance. It does not argue that plain-text continuity systems replace enterprise infrastructure in every setting. Rather, it argues that many of the same operational problems - context drift, stale authority, unsafe mutation, weak handoff, and loss of salience - can be addressed at the interface layer through human-readable objects carrying role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The paper frames Artificial Tangibility as a low-infrastructure governance layer for discontinuous AI collaboration: a way of making project state visible, bounded, auditable, and recoverable without requiring the runtime to possess human-like memory, embodiment, or consciousness. Its contribution is not the invention of memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, or agent tooling, but the synthesis of those concerns into a practical object grammar for AI continuity. Keywords: AI continuity, context engineering, human-AI interaction, AI state management, object-oriented cognition, agent memory, provenance, AI governance, durable execution 1. Introduction: From Theory to Operational Comparison Artificial Tangibility argues that AI runtimes do not need human embodiment, emotion, or persistent personal memory in order to participate usefully in long-running work. They need a usable interface into project state. That interface must make the work legible as bounded objects rather than as an undifferentiated pile of context. This companion paper asks a narrower applied question: how does that claim relate to the systems that AI engineers already use to manage state, memory, retrieval, orchestration, provenance, and human oversight? The answer is not that a file-based continuity system is identical to enterprise infrastructure. It is not. Durable execution engines, vector databases, event logs, checkpointers, orchestration graphs, and access-control systems perform technical functions that plain documents do not automatically provide. The stronger and safer claim is functional: Artificial Tangibility describes a human-readable governance layer that addresses many of the same failure pressures at the level where humans and AI runtimes actually coordinate. The practical problem is continuity across discontinuity. A runtime enters a project without lived memory of the prior work. It may have access to documents, chat logs, files, and instructions, but still lack orientation. It may know the topic while misunderstanding what is current, what is source, what is draft, what is blocked, what is permitted, and what should happen next. This is the problem of context without shape. Industry systems respond to this problem with memory architectures, retrieval systems, tool loops, checkpoints, event stores, blackboard patterns, and human-in-the-loop gates. Artificial Tangibility responds by shaping the project environment into objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The difference is not whether state matters. Both approaches assume that it does. The difference is where governance becomes visible and how much of that governance can be made human-readable. 2. Context Engineering and the Problem of Orientation Context engineering treats the context window as an engineered operating surface rather than a passive prompt box. That shift is important. It recognizes that the quality, order, scope, and structure of information supplied to an AI system can matter as much as the size of the model or the cleverness of the prompt. Artificial Tangibility begins from the same pressure point but states it in operational language: more context is not the same as more orientation. A project may contain all relevant files and still be unusable to a fresh runtime if the system fails to distinguish source from draft, active from parked, current from stale, or safe action from unauthorized mutation. The paper therefore moves from information volume to project shape. A context window may contain a useful source, an obsolete draft, a rejected route, a private note, a public claim, and a warning. If those items are not marked as different kinds of objects, the runtime must infer their status from prose, recency, style, or proximity. That is where coherent misalignment begins. The value of Artificial Tangibility is that it turns context management into object governance. A bounded object is not merely a piece of retrieved text. It carries a declared role. It carries authority status. It carries boundaries. It carries relation to other objects. It may carry an evidence trail. It may carry weight. These fields reduce the runtime's need to guess what the object is allowed to mean. 3. RAG, External Memory, and Source Authority Retrieval-augmented generation and related memory systems establish an important principle: a runtime should not rely only on internal model weights or conversational memory. It should be able to consult external materials. That principle is compatible with Artificial Tangibility. The difference is that retrieval alone does not determine authority. A retrieved document may be relevant and still not govern the current task. It may be historical, superseded, speculative, private, or parked. Artificial Tangibility therefore asks an additional question: once an object is retrieved, what is it allowed to do? This is where source authority becomes central. In a governed project, an object can exist without being promoted. A receipt can prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft can be useful without governing later work. A source can be current in one lane and irrelevant in another. The system must expose those distinctions before the runtime acts. In this sense, Artificial Tangibility is not a replacement for retrieval. It is a governance layer around retrieved and preserved material. It helps determine whether a retrieved object should be trusted, quoted, ignored, archived, used as background, or treated as the active source for the next move. 4. Agent Memory and Externalized Project State Modern agent-memory systems often distinguish working memory, episodic memory, and semantic memory. The project must carry continuity outside the runtime so that a future runtime can re-enter without requiring the human to rebuild the whole room. 5. Those systems persist state so the process can resume. Artificial Tangibility approaches recoverability from the interface side. This is the purpose of a re-entry test. A continuity system is working if a runtime can enter from a minimal orientation object and recover the state of the project without relying on the prior chat session. It should be able to answer: What is active? What governs? What is blocked? What must not be touched? What happened last? What should happen next? Those are established traditions. The claim is narrower and, for that reason, stronger: long-running AI collaboration needs a human-readable governance layer that binds these concerns together at the level of project work. This matters because much AI collaboration occurs outside carefully engineered enterprise platforms. For those contexts, a low-infrastructure continuity grammar can make complex AI-assisted work more recoverable without pretending that the runtime is continuous, embodied, conscious, or human. The companion claim can therefore be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility does not replace AI state-management infrastructure. It makes the governance problem legible. CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority

CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. candidates.body_html:
Canonical Tokens A Minimal Representatio

Canonical Tokens Canonical Tokens: A Minimal-Representation Principle for AI-Assisted Continuity Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract AI-assisted continuity work spends real, avoidable cost re-explaining references that are already at their minimal possible form. A number does not become more precise by being spelled out in longer language; it is already its own shortest correct description. An established name, once assigned, carries its referent without needing to be redefined at each use. This paper proposes the canonical token principle: certain references - numbers, assigned names, and fixed coordinate handles - should be treated as representationally complete once established, and re-expanding them in later context is waste rather than clarity. The paper grounds this claim in algorithmic information theory, where the shortest correct description of an object is a well- defined and long-studied quantity, and extends it into AI-assisted project work through the Authority concept already proposed in Continuity, Authority, Directive. It also confronts a genuine complication directly: current large language model tokenizers do not reliably treat numbers as stable, canonical units internally, which produces measurable arithmetic errors. This paper’s claim operates at a different layer - the documentation and prompting layer, not the tokenizer’s internal representation - and the paper is explicit about that boundary rather than overstating what it fixes. Keywords: AI continuity, minimum description length, Kolmogorov complexity, canonical representation, tokenization, context efficiency, AI state management, object-oriented cognition This is the fourth paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) proposes that bounded objects give non-embodied AI runtimes operational grip. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that proposal against existing AI state-management patterns. Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposes a control grammar for governing those objects. This paper narrows further, to a single governance question those earlier papers assume but do not resolve: once a reference is established, when should it ever need to be re-explained? 1. The Problem: Re-Explaining What Is Already Minimal Long-running AI-assisted work regularly wastes effort re-describing things that cannot be described more efficiently than they already are. A number is the clearest case. Three is already three. There is no shorter, more precise way to refer to the quantity three than the token that already means three. Spelling out “the third item in the sequence” instead of writing “3” does not add precision. It adds length without adding information. A name behaves the same way once it is assigned. If a person, object, or coordinate has been given a stable name, that name is already a complete, minimal reference to the thing it names. Re-explaining who or what the name refers to every time it appears is not caution. It is redundant expansion of something that was already at its shortest correct form. This matters more in AI-assisted work than it might first appear, for a reason specific to how these systems operate. Every re-explanation is not free. It occupies context, competes with other material for the runtime’s attention, and in genuinely long or multi-document work, contributes directly to the same context-without-shape problem described elsewhere in this sequence (Gelhaus, 2026a, 2026b). A project that repeatedly re-spells-out numbers, re-defines established names, or re-explains fixed coordinates is paying a real, cumulative cost for information that did not need to be resupplied. The claim of this paper is narrow and specific: certain references are already canonical. Once established, they should be treated as complete, not as invitations to re-explain. 2. Canonical Form Has a Real, Existing Definition This is not a new idea invented for AI-assisted work. It has a name and a long history in information theory: the shortest correct description of an object, below which no further compression is possible without losing information, is formalized as Kolmogorov complexity, introduced as one of three approaches to a quantitative definition of information (Kolmogorov, 1965). A number’s own digit representation is at or near this floor for the overwhelming majority of practical purposes - there is no shorter correct way to specify the number 3 than a token that means 3. The related Minimum Description Length principle extends this from individual objects to entire models: the best description of a body of data is the one that minimizes the combined length of the model and the data described through it (Rissanen, 1978). Applied to project documentation rather than statistical modeling, the same logic holds: the best record of a project state is not the one that repeats the most detail, but the one that encodes established references at their minimal form and spends its remaining length on what is actually new. This grounding matters because it keeps the claim honest and bounded. This paper is not arguing that shorter is always better, or that all context should be compressed indiscriminately. It is arguing something much narrower: a specific, well-defined class of references - fixed numbers, assigned names, established coordinate handles - are already at or near their representational floor, and treating them as if they need further unpacking is a documented, named category of waste, not a stylistic preference. 3. Canonical Tokens as an Authority State Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposed Authority as the field that tells a runtime what a given object’s status is: current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted. This paper proposes that canonical tokens deserve their own authority state, distinct from the others: established and complete. An object with this status is not a draft awaiting revision, nor a source awaiting promotion. It is a reference that has already reached its minimal correct form and requires no further processing to be trusted. A number is established and complete the moment it is written. A name is established and complete the moment it is assigned and recorded once, in an index or reference list, the same way a receipt or Blackboard already functions elsewhere in this sequence. This has a direct practical consequence for AI-assisted work: once a runtime has seen a canonical token defined - a name assigned to a person, a coordinate assigned to an object, a number stated in context - it should treat later appearances of that same token as already resolved, not as an occasion to redefine, re-describe, or expand. The correct action on encountering an established canonical token again is to use it, not to re-explain it. This is consistent with, and a direct extension of, a rule already present informally in this project’s own working practice: a short, stable handle carries the reference, while the meaning of that handle lives once, in an index, rather than being repeated at every point of use. What this paper adds is the theoretical grounding for why that rule works - not merely as a convenient habit, but as an application of a well- established, decades-old principle about the floor of correct description. 4. A Genuine Complication: Tokenizers Do Not Yet Honor This Principle Internally Any paper making a claim this clean about numbers deserves to be tested against what actually happens inside the systems it is written for. The honest answer is that current large language model tokenizers do not reliably treat numbers as stable, canonical units at all. Standard byte-pair-encoding tokenizers frequently split numbers inconsistently: one three-digit number may be represented as a single token while a neighboring three- digit number is split across two or three tokens, depending on how frequently that specific digit sequence appeared during training rather than on any property of the number itself (Singh and Strouse, 2024). This is not a minor cosmetic issue. The same research demonstrates that this inconsistency produces measurable, stereotyped arithmetic errors, and that changing the tokenization direction or forcing consistent digit grouping (for example, by inserting separators) measurably improves accuracy. This is a real complication, and it should not be minimized or explained away. It means that at the level of the model’s internal representation, the number 3 and the number 703 are not treated with the same kind of canonical stability this paper is arguing for at the documentation layer. The floor this paper describes is a property of the number itself, in principle; it is not yet a property reliably respected by the tokenizer that turns that number into the units a model actually computes over. The honest resolution is to be precise about which layer this paper’s claim operates on. It is a claim about the documentation and prompting layer: how humans and AI-assisted systems should treat already- established references in the text of a project - project notes, handoff files, receipts, source maps - regardless of how a given tokenizer happens to segment that text internally. A canonical token, once established in a project’s documentation, should not be re-expanded in later prose even if the model’s own tokenizer is, at a lower level, still doing something less clean with the underlying digits. The two problems are related in spirit - both are about respecting a stable, minimal representation - but they are not the same problem, and this paper does not claim to solve both. 5. The Practical Rule The operational rule this paper proposes is simple to state and directly testable: establish a canonical token once, in an index or reference object, and treat every later appearance of that same token as already resolved. For numbers, this means not re-deriving or re-explaining a quantity once it has been stated - referring back to it directly rather than restating its derivation or spelling it out in longer language. For names, this means assigning a name once, recording what it refers to in a single place, and using the bare name afterward rather than re-describing the referent at each use. For coordinate handles - the short, machine-facing identifiers used elsewhere in this sequence to name objects, lanes, and receipts - this means treating the handle itself as the canonical reference, with its meaning living once in an index rather than being re-explained inline every time the handle is used. The failure mode this rule prevents is cumulative rather than dramatic. No single re- explanation of an established token is very costly. But a project that habitually re- derives, re-describes, or re-spells-out already-established references pays that cost repeatedly, and in long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime work, that repeated cost is exactly the kind of unstructured burden the rest of this sequence has already argued against (Gelhaus, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c). 6. Boundary Conditions and Limits This principle applies specifically to references that are genuinely already minimal: fixed numbers, assigned names, and established coordinate handles. It does not apply to descriptions, arguments, or explanations, which frequently do benefit from restatement, elaboration, or repetition for clarity. The claim is narrow on purpose. This paper also does not claim to resolve the tokenizer-level inconsistency documented in Section 4. That is a model-architecture and training-data problem, addressed by a separate and active line of research, not by project documentation discipline. Finally, this principle depends on the canonical token actually having been established clearly before it is reused. If a name or handle is introduced ambiguously, or if the same handle is later reused for a different referent, the principle breaks down - not because the principle is wrong, but because its precondition, a genuinely established and complete reference, was never actually met. This is the same kind of dependency on disciplined use already acknowledged for Continuity, Authority, and Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c): the grammar only works if the objects it governs are maintained honestly. 7. Evaluation Criteria This claim should be testable rather than merely plausible. Four criteria are proposed. First, context economy: a project that establishes canonical tokens once and reuses them without re-expansion should require measurably less context to convey the same information than one that re-explains established references repeatedly. Second, reduced drift: a runtime working from a project with clearly established canonical tokens should be less likely to introduce inconsistent restatements of the same number or name across a long document or a long multi-session project. Third, faster verification: a human reviewing project output should be able to check an established token against its single index entry more quickly than reconstructing its meaning from repeated, possibly slightly inconsistent, restatements scattered through the text. Fourth, clean failure: when a canonical token is misused - reused for a different referent, or contradicted by a later restatement - that failure should be easy to locate precisely because the correct behavior (use the established token without re- expansion) is simple and specific enough that a violation stands out clearly. 8. Conclusion Some references are already as short as they can correctly be. A number is its own minimal description. An assigned name, once recorded, is a complete reference to what it names. Treating these as things that must be re-explained on every appearance is not thoroughness. It is the accumulation of avoidable cost in exactly the kind of long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime AI-assisted work this sequence has been concerned with throughout. This paper grounds that observation in an existing, well-established idea - the floor of correct description, formalized decades ago in algorithmic information theory - rather than presenting it as a new invention. It extends Continuity, Authority, Directive by proposing a specific authority state for canonical tokens: established and complete, requiring no further processing once recorded. And it confronts, rather than avoids, the genuine complication that current tokenizers do not yet honor this principle at the level of internal model representation, drawing a clear boundary between what this paper’s discipline actually governs and what remains a separate, open research problem. The practical instruction is simple: name it once, record what it means once, and afterward, use the name. An established name, once assigned, carries its referent without needing to be redefined at each use. This paper proposes the canonical token principle: certain references - numbers, assigned names, and fixed coordinate handles - should be treated as representationally complete once established, and re-expanding them in later context is waste rather than clarity. The paper grounds this claim in algorithmic information theory, where the shortest correct description of an object is a well- defined and long-studied quantity, and extends it into AI-assisted project work through the Authority concept already proposed in Continuity, Authority, Directive. It also confronts a genuine complication directly: current large language model tokenizers do not reliably treat numbers as stable, canonical units internally, which produces measurable arithmetic errors. This paper’s claim operates at a different layer - the documentation and prompting layer, not the tokenizer’s internal representation - and the paper is explicit about that boundary rather than overstating what it fixes. Keywords: AI continuity, minimum description length, Kolmogorov complexity, canonical representation, tokenization, context efficiency, AI state management, object-oriented cognition This is the fourth paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) proposes that bounded objects give non-embodied AI runtimes operational grip. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that proposal against existing AI state-management patterns. Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposes a control grammar for governing those objects. This paper narrows further, to a single governance question those earlier papers assume but do not resolve: once a reference is established, when should it ever need to be re-explained? 1. A number is the clearest case. Three is already three. There is no shorter, more precise way to refer to the quantity three than the token that already means three. Spelling out “the third item in the sequence” instead of writing “3” does not add precision. It adds length without adding information. A name behaves the same way once it is assigned.
