candidates.body_html:
THE CONTRIBUTION IS NOT THE BYLINE

THE CONTRIBUTION IS NOT THE BYLINE

Role-Enacted Human–AI Collaboration, Intellectual Provenance, and Accountable Research

Benjamin Gelhaus | Independent researcher | Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC)

Public discussion working paper · Revised edition v1.1 · 7 November 2026

Developed in dialogue with Avishai Roif’s Ethical Use of AI in Academic Research, with a conceptual extension drawn from Functional Layers (29 October 2026).

Abstract

Research integrity depends on knowing both who takes responsibility for a final claim and how that claim developed. This paper proposes that the roles assigned to artificial intelligence—and enacted through the researcher's questions, responses, corrections, and willingness to reconsider—are functional variables that can influence the course of human–AI collaboration. A designation such as “tool,” “critic,” “instructor,” or “collaborator” establishes expectations; the way participants subsequently interact establishes how those expectations operate. The resulting feedback can affect which objections are raised, which proposals are pursued, and which revisions become part of the work. The thesis joins two complementary inquiries: intellectual provenance, which reconstructs who or what introduced, developed, checked, and adopted an idea; and role enactment, which investigates how the interaction produced those contributions. The proposal builds on the author's Functional Layers framework and emerged during an unexpected exchange about Avishai Roif's proposed ethics code. OOCC's historical-learning and source-recovery records supply illustrative cases involving copied AI explanations, conversation branches, preserved corrections, retrieval comparisons, and cross-index integrity. A prospective factorial experiment is proposed to separate the effects of role labels from enacted collaborative behavior and to assess scientific accuracy, constructive disagreement, correction uptake, and cost. The empirical value of these interventions remains a research question; their roles and outcomes can be made observable and tested.

Keywords: human–AI collaboration; role enactment; Functional Layers; intellectual provenance; scholarly authorship; feedback; research integrity; verification; source-governed continuity.

1. Research Question and Central Argument

The central problem is simple: academic authorship establishes who accepts responsibility for a publication, while intellectual provenance reconstructs how the underlying ideas were developed. Both matter for a credible research record. A paper can accurately identify its accountable author and still leave a reader uncertain about where a decisive objection, analogy, hypothesis, or revision entered the work.

This paper adds a second question. What determines which ideas are proposed and which criticisms become influential during collaboration? The author's working hypothesis is that interaction roles help condition those outcomes. Role designation establishes a set of expectations; role enactment reinforces or contradicts them through actual behavior; the feedback between participants shapes the next steps. These mechanisms can be studied by observing what changes when role labels, interaction rules, and responses to disagreement are varied while other conditions are held constant.

The paper therefore advances two linked propositions. First, intellectual contribution can be reconstructed as a source-linked history of origination, development, verification, and human acceptance. Second, the organization of the human–AI relationship may alter that history by changing the opportunities for criticism, inquiry, correction, and conceptual development. An accurate account of contribution examines both the events and the conditions in which they occurred.

2. A Scholarly Exchange That Sharpened the Question

Avishai Roif's discussion draft Ethical Use of AI in Academic Research (6 November 2026) centers accountability in the human researcher. Article 2 assigns responsibility for the claims in a paper to its author; Article 8 requires each consequential step of an argument to be justified and checked; Article 4 concerns AI as a research instrument; and Article 11 calls for disclosure of AI use. This structure supplies a useful foundation for understanding the ethical obligations that accompany AI-assisted work (Roif, 2026).

In a subsequent exchange with the author, Roif offered a clarification that materially improved the present argument: Article 2 asks the researcher to make the claim their own through understanding, adoption, and verification; it does not demand that the researcher invented every initial idea. He also affirmed that AI interactions can be treated as research data when those interactions are themselves being studied. That clarification resolves a significant portion of the initial interpretive disagreement.

Roif then posed a more difficult question: if AI's use is described through the methods and disclosure, what does the designation “contributor” add? His analogy was to a satellite, calculator, or search engine. The present paper accepts the distinction between institutional authorship and the description of an instrument's use, then asks whether a role description can itself affect the behavior of the research process. The term “collaborator” may function as an interaction instruction as well as a descriptive label.

The distinction is practical. Calling an AI a collaborator can cue expectations of initiative, criticism, alternative hypotheses, and reciprocal revision. Calling it a calculator can cue expectations of narrow execution and a final answer. Actual treatment is equally consequential: a researcher who declares openness to criticism but dismisses every inconvenient finding enacts a directive relationship; a researcher who invites criticism, evaluates it, and updates a claim enacts a collaborative relationship. The designation and the enacted behavior are separately observable.

This reframes the conversation as a shared research opportunity. Roif's question directs attention to the standards by which a human researcher adopts a claim. Functional Layers directs attention to the interaction conditions that influence how the claim develops. Together they invite an empirical investigation of whether, when, and how research outcomes change.

3. Role Assignment and Role Enactment

A functional role is an assignment of expected operations within a larger process. A research assistant retrieves relevant information; a critic challenges assumptions; an instructor builds comprehension; a collaborator shares a sustained inquiry through proposals, objections, revisions, and evidence checks. The same model may be asked to perform several roles, but performance depends on its capabilities, source access, governing constraints, and the exchange that follows.

Three variables make the role observable. Assigned role records the explicit designation and instructions provided to the AI. Enacted role records how the human and AI actually behave across turns: whether questions permit disagreement, whether mistakes are acknowledged, whether alternatives are examined, and whether criticism can affect the next action. Observed contribution records what happened: a relevant objection, changed argument, corrected calculation, rejected hypothesis, verified source, or altered decision.

The enacted role belongs to both participants. A human researcher can request candid criticism and then refuse every correction. Conversely, an AI can be described as a tool while the researcher consistently invites open criticism and thoughtful revision. The label, the instructions, and the human's behavior may therefore have separable effects. Their interaction is the experimental target.

An everyday principle captures the point: actions speak louder than words. A stated collaborative role gains functional meaning when the participants repeatedly enact it. That interaction can make disagreement a useful contribution to the work rather than a failure to satisfy an expected answer. A correction becomes valuable when the researcher examines it, checks the supporting evidence, and decides what to change.

The proposed term is role-conditioned functional behavior: differences in observable operations and research outcomes associated with explicit role designation, enacted interaction expectations, and feedback practices under matched conditions. The claim is causal in ambition and conditional in scope. The experiment should identify which mechanism matters, for which tasks, and at what cost.

4. Functional Layers: A Framework for Investigating the Relationship

The author's Functional Layers research, documented in an R4 evidence-first edition dated 29 October 2026, investigates whether the causal organization of interacting functions can produce capabilities that are poorly described by listing components in isolation. Its unit of explanation is the relationship among functions: direction of influence, timing, feedback, persistent state, constraints, and the effect on later decisions (Gelhaus, 2026, Functional Layers).

The framework provides an operational way to examine the present question. A researcher asks a question; an AI generates a candidate; the researcher responds; a correction may alter subsequent retrieval; the next response may then differ. A collaborative role is expressed through this sequence of interactions. The important variables are what information moves between the participants, what each participant does with it, and what changes when feedback is removed, delayed, or reorganized.

Functional Layers also treats the human as part of the interacting research system whenever the human is actively guiding inquiry. That matters in the current case. The researcher's willingness to entertain a disconfirming result may be as important as the model's ability to produce one. Measuring AI output alone would leave part of the mechanism unexamined.

The Functional Layers manuscript already proposes comparisons between linked and isolated processes, persistent and missing corrections, human-guided and automated retrieval, and connected and disconnected workflows. Role enactment supplies an additional relational intervention: keep the task and model constant while changing the way the human and AI organize criticism, acceptance, and follow-up. An improvement in accuracy, useful corrections, or conceptual development would then motivate deeper causal testing.

The framework also identifies relevant tradeoffs. Directness, speed, creativity, factual fidelity, user effort, and conversational openness may respond differently to the same intervention. A collaborative treatment might improve error detection while increasing time spent deliberating; it might stimulate more alternatives while making final decisions harder. The research should report these dimensions separately.

5. The Accidental Development of This Thesis

The paper's own history illustrates why role and provenance belong together. The author began with a disagreement about whether institutional recognition determines the occurrence of an intellectual contribution. He asked an AI assistant to help develop a public reply to Roif's paper. The assistant suggested historical examples involving Semmelweis, Wegener, Marshall, and Warren and challenged an overgeneralized claim about institutional motives. The author accepted the correction while retaining his original argument.

That exchange expanded into a discussion of practical research capacity, the author's learning history, and the OOCC archive. The human requested that selected evidence be assembled for scholarly inspection. A seven-document review packet was prepared and shared; the discussion unexpectedly produced a separate thesis about accountable authorship and intellectual provenance. The author then recognized that the new paper had emerged through precisely the kind of human–AI interaction it described.

Roif's thoughtful reply generated a further revision. His clarification of Article 2 narrowed the doctrinal disagreement. His challenge about the word “contributor” prompted the human to connect the exchange to Functional Layers and to articulate a new insight: a designation establishes a role, while the human's actions and the continuing feedback enact that role. The present revised edition records this change as an identifiable step in the thesis's development.

Within the visible exchange, the human supplied the central argument, selected research directions, decided which qualifications to accept, authorized publication, and initiated the new hypothesis. The AI contributed candidate examples, criticism, comparison ideas, editorial structure, and draft language. Roif's external response provided a substantive corrective and a motivating question. This qualitative record demonstrates a traceable development sequence; an independently frozen and consented conversation archive would support finer-grained scientific analysis of timing and causal attribution.

6. Source-Grounded Cases from OOCC

OOCC's archival and crawler work provides practical examples for studying provenance and interaction. The reported cases below retain their original scope. They are research leads and bounded findings drawn from dated source work. The public OOCC review packet offers curated case summaries and an evidence register; restricted records can be assessed through an appropriately authorized source-review process.

6.1. Original wording and later reuse

A Human Learning Crawler (HLC) case describes an original human recovery analogy, an assistant's technical explanation, and later reuse of AI wording in a human-role message. The sequence makes attribution a question of event history rather than the apparent speaker of a single later excerpt. The case invites a source-level check of which ideas originated where, how they were developed, and how the human subsequently used the explanation.

6.2. Multiple branches and correction history

Crawler A10 reported ten selected conversation-graph checks comprising 1,592 mapped nodes, including 1,411 nodes along selected-current ancestry and 181 outside that path. Such offpath records can contain alternative attempts, abandoned hypotheses, and corrections. A depth-crawler case separately preserved the distinction between an assistant's acknowledgment of a requested lossless reorganization and independent evidence of a completed result. These findings motivate procedures that track both the path followed and the conditions needed to verify it.

6.3. Negative retrieval results

A V3 retrospective comparison reported directly relevant retrieval results of 4/35 for literal search, 6/35 for expanded search, and 3/35 for graph-hop retrieval. In that scoped sample, expanded retrieval performed best. Keeping this finding visible helps prevent the attraction of a sophisticated relational method from becoming a substitute for comparative evaluation.

6.4. Agreement between indexes

An OOCC intersection report recorded matching sets of 673 unique association identifiers across two parsed views. It also distinguished identical mirrored records from independent confirmation. The result provides a case for testing record consistency and a reminder to validate the meanings of relationships separately from their identifier integrity.

These cases show why a detailed contribution record can be useful. They also offer concrete tasks for a controlled study: detecting copied authorship, recovering omitted alternatives, evaluating a correction, selecting an effective retrieval method, and distinguishing consistent records from independent evidence.

7. A Provenance Record with Role Context

The original paper proposed an Origin–Development–Verification–Responsibility (ODVR) record. The revised theory retains those four elements and adds role context as a relational field recorded across them. The resulting representation preserves both what happened and how the participants' operating expectations influenced its development.

Origin records the earliest observed appearance of a candidate idea within a defined source collection, including the original actor or message role and any preceding question. Development records substantive modifications, objections, alternatives, and feedback. Verification records the source reads, calculations, tests, and independent checks actually performed. Responsibility records the human researcher who evaluated, adopted, revised, or rejected the claim and accepted responsibility for its publication.

Role context adds the initial designation, active instructions, actual human treatment, critical-feedback opportunities, corrections, and subsequent changes in direction. For example, a source-linked record might show that an AI was explicitly invited to challenge a proposed explanation; the AI raised a specific objection; the human checked a cited source, accepted part of the criticism, and revised the hypothesis. The record could also show that the human dismissed a criticism or that the assistant's proposed objection failed verification.

Each recorded event should preserve source identity, revision, participant role, sequence, relation to predecessor events, evidence status, and the researcher's disposition. Where the available corpus starts after the idea first appeared or source access is restricted, the record specifies that boundary. This is important because a local earliest appearance establishes a source position within the collected material; a literature-wide originality claim requires separate research.

8. A Direct Experiment: Does the Assigned and Enacted Role Matter?

The initial demonstration is deliberately simple. Present two fresh instances of the same AI model with the same research task and materials. In the collaborative condition, encourage candid disagreement, independent alternatives, criticism of weak assumptions, and reciprocal examination of objections. In the directive condition, frame the model as a narrowly instructed instrument carrying out the researcher's chosen plan. Compare the quality of the work, including the human's subsequent decisions. This practical demonstration is the invitation emerging from the discussion with Roif.

A stronger experiment distinguishes the effects of words from the effects of treatment. Use a two-by-two design with two labels—“tool” and “collaborator”—crossed with two interaction practices—directive and critical-dialogic. In the directive condition, the human asks for task execution and provides tightly scoped follow-up. In the dialogic condition, the human requests objections, checks proposed alternatives, and responds substantively when the AI disagrees. All conditions preserve factual accuracy requirements, honest uncertainty, and researcher accountability.

Recruit participants or use carefully standardized human interaction scripts, and counterbalance assignment across comparable tasks. Match models, context, source access, task difficulty, time budgets, and tool permissions. Record the messages and explicit role instructions with consent. Include deliberate false premises, incomplete arguments, conflicting sources, and open-ended hypothesis development. Independent reviewers should assess outcome quality using preregistered criteria while blind to the experimental condition where feasible.

Primary outcomes include justified disagreement rate, useful error detection, factual accuracy, evidence fidelity, uptake of valid corrections, quality of the final human judgment, and the number of unsupported confident claims. Secondary outcomes include diversity of hypotheses, perceived collaborative usefulness, participant learning on held-out tasks, latency, and total verification labor. Report human and model effort together.

The factorial design supports four useful interpretations. A label effect would suggest that designation itself matters. An enactment effect would suggest that interaction behavior matters even when labels differ. An interaction effect would suggest that words and treatment reinforce one another. Weak or mixed effects would clarify the situations in which the approach offers value. These outcomes can refine the Functional Layers account and help distinguish a real causal mechanism from a memorable anecdote.

The resulting research program contains two related comparisons. The first examines how interaction roles affect the development of claims. The second examines whether ODVR plus role-context records enable third-party reviewers to reconstruct those claims more accurately than competent summaries, full-text search, and strong modern source-linked memory. One experiment investigates production; the other investigates preservation and auditability.

9. Implications for Research Integrity

Roif's position provides a useful separation of duties: the human researcher adopts and answers for the final research claim. The present proposal examines how that claim was developed, which relationships contributed to its development, and how much detail a methods or disclosure statement should preserve. These inquiries can coexist within a human-accountable publication practice.

A general disclosure identifying ChatGPT as an assistant communicates the presence of a tool. A role-aware research history can further communicate that the author invited adversarial review, that a specific objection changed the argument, and that the human verified the resulting correction. The key practical proposition is therefore direct: describing an AI's role influences expectations, enacting that role through conduct influences feedback, and measuring the resulting changes can reveal what forms of interaction improve research. Scholarly rules can continue to specify who signs and defends the manuscript while methodology records the functional history that preceded the signature.

A name can assign a role, but the relationship gives that role its practical meaning. A researcher who welcomes criticism, verifies objections, and is prepared to revise a claim establishes different interaction conditions from one who asks only for execution of a predetermined task. The causal effects of those conditions can be examined with matched experiments.

The original question of this thesis was who contributed what to an idea. The revised question is also how the working relationship influenced what was contributed. THE CONTRIBUTION IS NOT THE BYLINE
THE CONTRIBUTION IS NOT THE BYLINE
Role-Enacted Human–AI Collaboration, Intellectual Provenance, and Accountable Research
Benjamin Gelhaus | Independent researcher | Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC)
Public discussion working paper · Revised edition v1.1 · 7 November 2026
Developed in dialogue with Avishai Roif’s Ethical Use of AI in Academic Research, with a conceptual extension drawn from Functional Layers (29 October 2026).
Abstract
Research integrity depends on knowing both who takes responsibility for a final claim and how that claim developed. This paper proposes that the roles assigned to artificial intelligence—and enacted through the researcher's questions, responses, corrections, and willingness to reconsider—are functional variables that can influence the course of human–AI collaboration. A designation such as “tool,” “critic,” “instructor,” or “collaborator” establishes expectations; the way participants subsequently interact establishes how those expectations operate. The resulting feedback can affect which objections are raised, which proposals are pursued, and which revisions become part of the work. The thesis joins two complementary inquiries: intellectual provenance, which reconstructs who or what introduced, developed, checked, and adopted an idea; and role enactment, which investigates how the interaction produced those contributions. The proposal builds on the author's Functional Layers framework and emerged during an unexpected exchange about Avishai Roif's proposed ethics code. OOCC's historical-learning and source-recovery records supply illustrative cases involving copied AI explanations, conversation branches, preserved corrections, retrieval comparisons, and cross-index integrity. A prospective factorial experiment is proposed to separate the effects of role labels from enacted collaborative behavior and to assess scientific accuracy, constructive disagreement, correction uptake, and cost. The empirical value of these interventions remains a research question; their roles and outcomes can be made observable and tested.
Keywords: human–AI collaboration; role enactment; Functional Layers; intellectual provenance; scholarly authorship; feedback; research integrity; verification; source-governed continuity.
1. Research Question and Central Argument
The central problem is simple: academic authorship establishes who accepts responsibility for a publication, while intellectual provenance reconstructs how the underlying ideas were developed. Both matter for a credible research record. A paper can accurately identify its accountable author and still leave a reader uncertain about where a decisive objection, analogy, hypothesis, or revision entered the work.
This paper adds a second question. What determines which ideas are proposed and which criticisms become influential during collaboration? The author's working hypothesis is that interaction roles help condition those outcomes. Role designation establishes a set of expectations; role enactment reinforces or contradicts them through actual behavior; the feedback between participants shapes the next steps. These mechanisms can be studied by observing what changes when role labels, interaction rules, and responses to disagreement are varied while other conditions are held constant.
The paper therefore advances two linked propositions. First, intellectual contribution can be reconstructed as a source-linked history of origination, development, verification, and human acceptance. Second, the organization of the human–AI relationship may alter that history by changing the opportunities for criticism, inquiry, correction, and conceptual development. An accurate account of contribution examines both the events and the conditions in which they occurred.
2. A Scholarly Exchange That Sharpened the Question
Avishai Roif's discussion draft Ethical Use of AI in Academic Research (6 November 2026) centers accountability in the human researcher. Article 2 assigns responsibility for the claims in a paper to its author; Article 8 requires each consequential step of an argument to be justified and checked; Article 4 concerns AI as a research instrument; and Article 11 calls for disclosure of AI use. This structure supplies a useful foundation for understanding the ethical obligations that accompany AI-assisted work (Roif, 2026).
In a subsequent exchange with the author, Roif offered a clarification that materially improved the present argument: Article 2 asks the researcher to make the claim their own through understanding, adoption, and verification; it does not demand that the researcher invented every initial idea. He also affirmed that AI interactions can be treated as research data when those interactions are themselves being studied. That clarification resolves a significant portion of the initial interpretive disagreement.
Roif then posed a more difficult question: if AI's use is described through the methods and disclosure, what does the designation “contributor” add? His analogy was to a satellite, calculator, or search engine. The present paper accepts the distinction between institutional authorship and the description of an instrument's use, then asks whether a role description can itself affect the behavior of the research process. The term “collaborator” may function as an interaction instruction as well as a descriptive label.
The distinction is practical. Calling an AI a collaborator can cue expectations of initiative, criticism, alternative hypotheses, and reciprocal revision. Calling it a calculator can cue expectations of narrow execution and a final answer. Actual treatment is equally consequential: a researcher who declares openness to criticism but dismisses every inconvenient finding enacts a directive relationship; a researcher who invites criticism, evaluates it, and updates a claim enacts a collaborative relationship. The designation and the enacted behavior are separately observable.
This reframes the conversation as a shared research opportunity. Roif's question directs attention to the standards by which a human researcher adopts a claim. Functional Layers directs attention to the interaction conditions that influence how the claim develops. Together they invite an empirical investigation of whether, when, and how research outcomes change.
3. Role Assignment and Role Enactment
A functional role is an assignment of expected operations within a larger process. A research assistant retrieves relevant information; a critic challenges assumptions; an instructor builds comprehension; a collaborator shares a sustained inquiry through proposals, objections, revisions, and evidence checks. The same model may be asked to perform several roles, but performance depends on its capabilities, source access, governing constraints, and the exchange that follows.
Three variables make the role observable. Assigned role records the explicit designation and instructions provided to the AI. Enacted role records how the human and AI actually behave across turns: whether questions permit disagreement, whether mistakes are acknowledged, whether alternatives are examined, and whether criticism can affect the next action. Observed contribution records what happened: a relevant objection, changed argument, corrected calculation, rejected hypothesis, verified source, or altered decision.
The enacted role belongs to both participants. A human researcher can request candid criticism and then refuse every correction. Conversely, an AI can be described as a tool while the researcher consistently invites open criticism and thoughtful revision. The label, the instructions, and the human's behavior may therefore have separable effects. Their interaction is the experimental target.
An everyday principle captures the point: actions speak louder than words. A stated collaborative role gains functional meaning when the participants repeatedly enact it. That interaction can make disagreement a useful contribution to the work rather than a failure to satisfy an expected answer. A correction becomes valuable when the researcher examines it, checks the supporting evidence, and decides what to change.
The proposed term is role-conditioned functional behavior: differences in observable operations and research outcomes associated with explicit role designation, enacted interaction expectations, and feedback practices under matched conditions. The claim is causal in ambition and conditional in scope. The experiment should identify which mechanism matters, for which tasks, and at what cost.
4. Functional Layers: A Framework for Investigating the Relationship
The author's Functional Layers research, documented in an R4 evidence-first edition dated 29 October 2026, investigates whether the causal organization of interacting functions can produce capabilities that are poorly described by listing components in isolation. Its unit of explanation is the relationship among functions: direction of influence, timing, feedback, persistent state, constraints, and the effect on later decisions (Gelhaus, 2026, Functional Layers).
The framework provides an operational way to examine the present question. A researcher asks a question; an AI generates a candidate; the researcher responds; a correction may alter subsequent retrieval; the next response may then differ. A collaborative role is expressed through this sequence of interactions. The important variables are what information moves between the participants, what each participant does with it, and what changes when feedback is removed, delayed, or reorganized.
Functional Layers also treats the human as part of the interacting research system whenever the human is actively guiding inquiry. That matters in the current case. The researcher's willingness to entertain a disconfirming result may be as important as the model's ability to produce one. Measuring AI output alone would leave part of the mechanism unexamined.
The Functional Layers manuscript already proposes comparisons between linked and isolated processes, persistent and missing corrections, human-guided and automated retrieval, and connected and disconnected workflows. Role enactment supplies an additional relational intervention: keep the task and model constant while changing the way the human and AI organize criticism, acceptance, and follow-up. An improvement in accuracy, useful corrections, or conceptual development would then motivate deeper causal testing.
The framework also identifies relevant tradeoffs. Directness, speed, creativity, factual fidelity, user effort, and conversational openness may respond differently to the same intervention. A collaborative treatment might improve error detection while increasing time spent deliberating; it might stimulate more alternatives while making final decisions harder. The research should report these dimensions separately.
5. The Accidental Development of This Thesis
The paper's own history illustrates why role and provenance belong together. The author began with a disagreement about whether institutional recognition determines the occurrence of an intellectual contribution. He asked an AI assistant to help develop a public reply to Roif's paper. The assistant suggested historical examples involving Semmelweis, Wegener, Marshall, and Warren and challenged an overgeneralized claim about institutional motives. The author accepted the correction while retaining his original argument.
That exchange expanded into a discussion of practical research capacity, the author's learning history, and the OOCC archive. The human requested that selected evidence be assembled for scholarly inspection. A seven-document review packet was prepared and shared; the discussion unexpectedly produced a separate thesis about accountable authorship and intellectual provenance. The author then recognized that the new paper had emerged through precisely the kind of human–AI interaction it described.
Roif's thoughtful reply generated a further revision. His clarification of Article 2 narrowed the doctrinal disagreement. His challenge about the word “contributor” prompted the human to connect the exchange to Functional Layers and to articulate a new insight: a designation establishes a role, while the human's actions and the continuing feedback enact that role. The present revised edition records this change as an identifiable step in the thesis's development.
Within the visible exchange, the human supplied the central argument, selected research directions, decided which qualifications to accept, authorized publication, and initiated the new hypothesis. The AI contributed candidate examples, criticism, comparison ideas, editorial structure, and draft language. Roif's external response provided a substantive corrective and a motivating question. This qualitative record demonstrates a traceable development sequence; an independently frozen and consented conversation archive would support finer-grained scientific analysis of timing and causal attribution.
6. Source-Grounded Cases from OOCC
OOCC's archival and crawler work provides practical examples for studying provenance and interaction. The reported cases below retain their original scope. They are research leads and bounded findings drawn from dated source work. The public OOCC review packet offers curated case summaries and an evidence register; restricted records can be assessed through an appropriately authorized source-review process.
6.1. Original wording and later reuse
A Human Learning Crawler (HLC) case describes an original human recovery analogy, an assistant's technical explanation, and later reuse of AI wording in a human-role message. The sequence makes attribution a question of event history rather than the apparent speaker of a single later excerpt. The case invites a source-level check of which ideas originated where, how they were developed, and how the human subsequently used the explanation.
6.2. Multiple branches and correction history
Crawler A10 reported ten selected conversation-graph checks comprising 1,592 mapped nodes, including 1,411 nodes along selected-current ancestry and 181 outside that path. Such offpath records can contain alternative attempts, abandoned hypotheses, and corrections. A depth-crawler case separately preserved the distinction between an assistant's acknowledgment of a requested lossless reorganization and independent evidence of a completed result. These findings motivate procedures that track both the path followed and the conditions needed to verify it.
6.3. Negative retrieval results
A V3 retrospective comparison reported directly relevant retrieval results of 4/35 for literal search, 6/35 for expanded search, and 3/35 for graph-hop retrieval. In that scoped sample, expanded retrieval performed best. Keeping this finding visible helps prevent the attraction of a sophisticated relational method from becoming a substitute for comparative evaluation.
6.4. Agreement between indexes
An OOCC intersection report recorded matching sets of 673 unique association identifiers across two parsed views. It also distinguished identical mirrored records from independent confirmation. The result provides a case for testing record consistency and a reminder to validate the meanings of relationships separately from their identifier integrity.
These cases show why a detailed contribution record can be useful. They also offer concrete tasks for a controlled study: detecting copied authorship, recovering omitted alternatives, evaluating a correction, selecting an effective retrieval method, and distinguishing consistent records from independent evidence.
7. A Provenance Record with Role Context
The original paper proposed an Origin–Development–Verification–Responsibility (ODVR) record. The revised theory retains those four elements and adds role context as a relational field recorded across them. The resulting representation preserves both what happened and how the participants' operating expectations influenced its development.
Origin records the earliest observed appearance of a candidate idea within a defined source collection, including the original actor or message role and any preceding question. Development records substantive modifications, objections, alternatives, and feedback. Verification records the source reads, calculations, tests, and independent checks actually performed. Responsibility records the human researcher who evaluated, adopted, revised, or rejected the claim and accepted responsibility for its publication.
Role context adds the initial designation, active instructions, actual human treatment, critical-feedback opportunities, corrections, and subsequent changes in direction. For example, a source-linked record might show that an AI was explicitly invited to challenge a proposed explanation; the AI raised a specific objection; the human checked a cited source, accepted part of the criticism, and revised the hypothesis. The record could also show that the human dismissed a criticism or that the assistant's proposed objection failed verification.
Each recorded event should preserve source identity, revision, participant role, sequence, relation to predecessor events, evidence status, and the researcher's disposition. Where the available corpus starts after the idea first appeared or source access is restricted, the record specifies that boundary. This is important because a local earliest appearance establishes a source position within the collected material; a literature-wide originality claim requires separate research.
8. A Direct Experiment: Does the Assigned and Enacted Role Matter?
The initial demonstration is deliberately simple. Present two fresh instances of the same AI model with the same research task and materials. In the collaborative condition, encourage candid disagreement, independent alternatives, criticism of weak assumptions, and reciprocal examination of objections. In the directive condition, frame the model as a narrowly instructed instrument carrying out the researcher's chosen plan. Compare the quality of the work, including the human's subsequent decisions. This practical demonstration is the invitation emerging from the discussion with Roif.
A stronger experiment distinguishes the effects of words from the effects of treatment. Use a two-by-two design with two labels—“tool” and “collaborator”—crossed with two interaction practices—directive and critical-dialogic. In the directive condition, the human asks for task execution and provides tightly scoped follow-up. In the dialogic condition, the human requests objections, checks proposed alternatives, and responds substantively when the AI disagrees. All conditions preserve factual accuracy requirements, honest uncertainty, and researcher accountability.
Recruit participants or use carefully standardized human interaction scripts, and counterbalance assignment across comparable tasks. Match models, context, source access, task difficulty, time budgets, and tool permissions. Record the messages and explicit role instructions with consent. Include deliberate false premises, incomplete arguments, conflicting sources, and open-ended hypothesis development. Independent reviewers should assess outcome quality using preregistered criteria while blind to the experimental condition where feasible.
Primary outcomes include justified disagreement rate, useful error detection, factual accuracy, evidence fidelity, uptake of valid corrections, quality of the final human judgment, and the number of unsupported confident claims. Secondary outcomes include diversity of hypotheses, perceived collaborative usefulness, participant learning on held-out tasks, latency, and total verification labor. Report human and model effort together.
The factorial design supports four useful interpretations. A label effect would suggest that designation itself matters. An enactment effect would suggest that interaction behavior matters even when labels differ. An interaction effect would suggest that words and treatment reinforce one another. Weak or mixed effects would clarify the situations in which the approach offers value. These outcomes can refine the Functional Layers account and help distinguish a real causal mechanism from a memorable anecdote.
The resulting research program contains two related comparisons. The first examines how interaction roles affect the development of claims. The second examines whether ODVR plus role-context records enable third-party reviewers to reconstruct those claims more accurately than competent summaries, full-text search, and strong modern source-linked memory. One experiment investigates production; the other investigates preservation and auditability.
9. Implications for Research Integrity
Roif's position provides a useful separation of duties: the human researcher adopts and answers for the final research claim. The Object as Filter The Object as Filte

The Object as Filter The Object as Filter: Holographic Return, AI Continuity, and Human-Readable Interfaces Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract This paper argues that a single structural pattern recurs across three domains usually treated as unrelated: biological perception, the foundations-of-physics debate over observation and reality, and AI-facing continuity architecture. In each domain, an overwhelming, undifferentiated field is made navigable not by receiving it in full, but by filtering it into bounded, action-relevant units. Perceptual interface theory argues that organisms do not perceive reality directly but through a fitness-tuned interface that discards nearly all available information. A body of foundational- physics work, most notably John Wheeler’s participatory universe proposal, has speculated that observation itself may be constitutive of legible physical reality rather than a passive report on a reality that already existed in full. Object-oriented AI continuity architecture, developed across a companion sequence of papers, argues that AI runtimes require bounded, authority-marked, relationally-situated objects rather than raw undifferentiated context in order to act safely and recoverably. This paper treats these three as structurally related instances of one pattern rather than as a single unified theory, and is explicit throughout about which claims are established, which are contested, and which remain the author’s own prior framework requiring further definition before public presentation. Keywords: interface theory of perception, attention and filtering, participatory universe, AI continuity, object-oriented cognition, philosophy of perception, foundations of physics, human-readable interfaces This is the fifth paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) and its companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) propose that bounded objects give AI runtimes operational grip on overwhelming context. Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposes a control grammar for governing those objects, and Canonical Tokens (Gelhaus, 2026d) proposes a minimal- representation principle for a specific class of them. This paper steps back from AI- facing architecture specifically to ask a broader question those four papers assume but do not examine directly: is the filtering pattern they describe for AI runtimes a special case of something more general, observed independently in other domains that have nothing to do with artificial intelligence? This paper’s claim is bounded rather than triumphant: the pattern recurs; the recurrence is worth naming; the recurrence does not, by itself, prove any single grand unifying theory of consciousness, reality, or mind. 1. One Pattern, Three Domains The pattern under examination has a simple shape. An undifferentiated field exists, containing far more information than any single act of engagement with it can use. Something happens to that field - evolutionary tuning, an act of measurement, a design choice - that converts an unusable totality into a bounded, navigable, action- relevant structure. The structure that results is not the field itself. It is a rendering of the field, shaped by what the receiving system can use. This paper examines three instances of that shape: biological perception, a contested but serious position within physics regarding observation and reality, and AI-facing project continuity. The claim of this paper is not that these three instances share a hidden underlying mechanism in any strong metaphysical sense. The claim is narrower and more defensible: they share a recognizable structural pattern, and that recurrence is worth documenting carefully, with the boundaries of each domain’s evidence kept visible rather than blurred together. 2. Perceptual Filtering: The Interface Theory of Perception Human perception does not present reality as it is. This is not a controversial claim within perceptual science; it is close to a starting assumption. The interface theory of perception goes further, arguing that perception is actively shaped by evolutionary fitness rather than by accuracy: an organism whose perceptual system reported the true structure of reality, rather than a simplified, fitness-relevant rendering of it, would in general be outcompeted by an organism whose perceptual system reported only what mattered for survival and reproduction, formalized through evolutionary game-theoretic simulations comparing fitness-tuned versus truth-tuned perceptual strategies (Hoffman, Singh, and Prakash, 2015; Hoffman, 2019). The often-used analogy is a computer desktop: a blue rectangular icon is not blue, rectangular, or located where it appears in any deep physical sense, but the icon is not a lie either. It is a functional interface that lets a user interact correctly with underlying complexity the user does not need to perceive directly in order to act successfully. Perception, on this view, works the same way: it is not a window onto reality, but an interface to it, and the interface is good exactly because it hides almost everything that is not immediately useful. This paper does not claim that the recurrence of one structural pattern across four domains proves any single underlying metaphysical theory - not conscious realism, not panpsychism, not a designed universe, not any specific theological position the author may hold elsewhere. That order of discovery matters. When a practical engineering fix, arrived at independently under real operational pressure, turns out to share its underlying shape with findings from perceptual science and foundational physics, the correct conclusion is not that one domain proves another. The correct conclusion is that the underlying problem - how a bounded system makes an overwhelming field usable - may be a genuinely general one, worth studying as its own subject, wherever it appears. 9. AI-facing continuity architecture filters an overwhelming project history into bounded, authority-marked objects a non- embodied runtime can safely act on. The strongest, most defensible version of this paper’s argument is the narrowest one: filtering an overwhelming field into a bounded, action-relevant rendering is not a trick unique to AI system design. It appears to be a general solution to a general problem, and AI continuity architecture is simply the newest place it has been rediscovered, this time by engineering necessity rather than by evolution or theoretical physics. Artificial Tangibility as a Low Infrastr
Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract This companion paper situates Artificial Tangibility in relation to contemporary AI state-management patterns, including context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, durable execution, event sourcing, blackboard coordination, and human-in-the-loop governance. It does not argue that plain-text continuity systems replace enterprise infrastructure in every setting. Rather, it argues that many of the same operational problems - context drift, stale authority, unsafe mutation, weak handoff, and loss of salience - can be addressed at the interface layer through human-readable objects carrying role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The paper frames Artificial Tangibility as a low-infrastructure governance layer for discontinuous AI collaboration: a way of making project state visible, bounded, auditable, and recoverable without requiring the runtime to possess human-like memory, embodiment, or consciousness. Its contribution is not the invention of memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, or agent tooling, but the synthesis of those concerns into a practical object grammar for AI continuity. Keywords: AI continuity, context engineering, human-AI interaction, AI state management, object-oriented cognition, agent memory, provenance, AI governance, durable execution 1. Introduction: From Theory to Operational Comparison Artificial Tangibility argues that AI runtimes do not need human embodiment, emotion, or persistent personal memory in order to participate usefully in long-running work. They need a usable interface into project state. That interface must make the work legible as bounded objects rather than as an undifferentiated pile of context. This companion paper asks a narrower applied question: how does that claim relate to the systems that AI engineers already use to manage state, memory, retrieval, orchestration, provenance, and human oversight? The answer is not that a file-based continuity system is identical to enterprise infrastructure. It is not. Durable execution engines, vector databases, event logs, checkpointers, orchestration graphs, and access-control systems perform technical functions that plain documents do not automatically provide. The stronger and safer claim is functional: Artificial Tangibility describes a human-readable governance layer that addresses many of the same failure pressures at the level where humans and AI runtimes actually coordinate. The practical problem is continuity across discontinuity. A runtime enters a project without lived memory of the prior work. It may have access to documents, chat logs, files, and instructions, but still lack orientation. It may know the topic while misunderstanding what is current, what is source, what is draft, what is blocked, what is permitted, and what should happen next. This is the problem of context without shape. Industry systems respond to this problem with memory architectures, retrieval systems, tool loops, checkpoints, event stores, blackboard patterns, and human-in-the-loop gates. Artificial Tangibility responds by shaping the project environment into objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The difference is not whether state matters. Both approaches assume that it does. The difference is where governance becomes visible and how much of that governance can be made human-readable. 2. Context Engineering and the Problem of Orientation Context engineering treats the context window as an engineered operating surface rather than a passive prompt box. That shift is important. It recognizes that the quality, order, scope, and structure of information supplied to an AI system can matter as much as the size of the model or the cleverness of the prompt. Artificial Tangibility begins from the same pressure point but states it in operational language: more context is not the same as more orientation. A project may contain all relevant files and still be unusable to a fresh runtime if the system fails to distinguish source from draft, active from parked, current from stale, or safe action from unauthorized mutation. The paper therefore moves from information volume to project shape. A context window may contain a useful source, an obsolete draft, a rejected route, a private note, a public claim, and a warning. If those items are not marked as different kinds of objects, the runtime must infer their status from prose, recency, style, or proximity. That is where coherent misalignment begins. The value of Artificial Tangibility is that it turns context management into object governance. A bounded object is not merely a piece of retrieved text. It carries a declared role. It carries authority status. It carries boundaries. It carries relation to other objects. It may carry an evidence trail. It may carry weight. These fields reduce the runtime's need to guess what the object is allowed to mean. 3. RAG, External Memory, and Source Authority Retrieval-augmented generation and related memory systems establish an important principle: a runtime should not rely only on internal model weights or conversational memory. It should be able to consult external materials. That principle is compatible with Artificial Tangibility. The difference is that retrieval alone does not determine authority. A retrieved document may be relevant and still not govern the current task. It may be historical, superseded, speculative, private, or parked. Artificial Tangibility therefore asks an additional question: once an object is retrieved, what is it allowed to do? This is where source authority becomes central. In a governed project, an object can exist without being promoted. A receipt can prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft can be useful without governing later work. A source can be current in one lane and irrelevant in another. The system must expose those distinctions before the runtime acts. In this sense, Artificial Tangibility is not a replacement for retrieval. It is a governance layer around retrieved and preserved material. It helps determine whether a retrieved object should be trusted, quoted, ignored, archived, used as background, or treated as the active source for the next move. 4. Agent Memory and Externalized Project State Modern agent-memory systems often distinguish working memory, episodic memory, and semantic memory. They do this through databases, vector stores, summaries, thread identifiers, or memory-management policies. Artificial Tangibility expresses a related distinction in plain project terms. A live state board or orientation object functions as working memory: it tells the runtime what is active now. Receipts and communication logs function as episodic memory: they preserve what happened, what changed, what failed, and what remains open. Source-authority objects function as semantic control: they declare which materials govern the present work. The important point is not that files are technically equivalent to databases. They are not. The point is that the human-readable object-world can expose the same categories of state that more technical systems manage implicitly or programmatically. For a solo researcher, small team, or cross-tool workflow, that visibility can be more valuable than hidden sophistication. The method also avoids a common failure in long-running AI work: asking the runtime to remember the project. Artificial Tangibility assumes the runtime is discontinuous. The project must carry continuity outside the runtime so that a future runtime can re-enter without requiring the human to rebuild the whole room. 5. Durable Execution, Re-Entry, and Recoverability Production-grade agent systems often use checkpointers, orchestration engines, and durable execution platforms to recover from crashes, timeouts, rate limits, and incomplete workflows. Those systems persist state so the process can resume. Artificial Tangibility approaches recoverability from the interface side. The question is not only whether a process can resume automatically, but whether a fresh runtime can identify the active object, governing source, unresolved blockers, boundaries, and next safe action. This is the purpose of a re-entry test. Artificial Tangibility responds by shaping the project environment into objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The difference is not whether state matters. Both approaches assume that it does. The difference is where governance becomes visible and how much of that governance can be made human-readable. 2. It carries authority status. It carries boundaries. It carries relation to other objects. It may carry an evidence trail. It may carry weight. These fields reduce the runtime's need to guess what the object is allowed to mean. 3. RAG, External Memory, and Source Authority Retrieval-augmented generation and related memory systems establish an important principle: a runtime should not rely only on internal model weights or conversational memory. It should be able to consult external materials. That principle is compatible with Artificial Tangibility. The difference is that retrieval alone does not determine authority. A retrieved document may be relevant and still not govern the current task. It may be historical, superseded, speculative, private, or parked. Artificial Tangibility therefore asks an additional question: once an object is retrieved, what is it allowed to do? This is where source authority becomes central. In a governed project, an object can exist without being promoted. A receipt can prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft can be useful without governing later work. A source can be current in one lane and irrelevant in another. The system must expose those distinctions before the runtime acts. In this sense, Artificial Tangibility is not a replacement for retrieval. It is a governance layer around retrieved and preserved material. It helps determine whether a retrieved object should be trusted, quoted, ignored, archived, used as background, or treated as the active source for the next move. 4. A live state board or orientation object functions as working memory: it tells the runtime what is active now. Receipts and communication logs function as episodic memory: they preserve what happened, what changed, what failed, and what remains open. Source-authority objects function as semantic control: they declare which materials govern the present work. The important point is not that files are technically equivalent to databases. They are not. The point is that the human-readable object-world can expose the same categories of state that more technical systems manage implicitly or programmatically. Rather, it argues that many of the same operational problems - context drift, stale authority, unsafe mutation, weak handoff, and loss of salience - can be addressed at the interface layer through human-readable objects carrying role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The paper frames Artificial Tangibility as a low-infrastructure governance layer for discontinuous AI collaboration: a way of making project state visible, bounded, auditable, and recoverable without requiring the runtime to possess human-like memory, embodiment, or consciousness. Its contribution is not the invention of memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, or agent tooling, but the synthesis of those concerns into a practical object grammar for AI continuity. Keywords: AI continuity, context engineering, human-AI interaction, AI state management, object-oriented cognition, agent memory, provenance, AI governance, durable execution 1. Introduction: From Theory to Operational Comparison Artificial Tangibility argues that AI runtimes do not need human embodiment, emotion, or persistent personal memory in order to participate usefully in long-running work. They need a usable interface into project state. That interface must make the work legible as bounded objects rather than as an undifferentiated pile of context. This companion paper asks a narrower applied question: how does that claim relate to the systems that AI engineers already use to manage state, memory, retrieval, orchestration, provenance, and human oversight? The answer is not that a file-based continuity system is identical to enterprise infrastructure. It is not. Durable execution engines, vector databases, event logs, checkpointers, orchestration graphs, and access-control systems perform technical functions that plain documents do not automatically provide. The stronger and safer claim is functional: Artificial Tangibility describes a human-readable governance layer that addresses many of the same failure pressures at the level where humans and AI runtimes actually coordinate. The practical problem is continuity across discontinuity. A runtime enters a project without lived memory of the prior work. It may have access to documents, chat logs, files, and instructions, but still lack orientation. It may know the topic while misunderstanding what is current, what is source, what is draft, what is blocked, what is permitted, and what should happen next. This is the problem of context without shape. Industry systems respond to this problem with memory architectures, retrieval systems, tool loops, checkpoints, event stores, blackboard patterns, and human-in-the-loop gates. Artificial Tangibility responds by shaping the project environment into objects with declared role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. The difference is not whether state matters. Both approaches assume that it does. The difference is where governance becomes visible and how much of that governance can be made human-readable. 2. Context Engineering and the Problem of Orientation Context engineering treats the context window as an engineered operating surface rather than a passive prompt box. That shift is important. It recognizes that the quality, order, scope, and structure of information supplied to an AI system can matter as much as the size of the model or the cleverness of the prompt. Artificial Tangibility begins from the same pressure point but states it in operational language: more context is not the same as more orientation. A project may contain all relevant files and still be unusable to a fresh runtime if the system fails to distinguish source from draft, active from parked, current from stale, or safe action from unauthorized mutation. The paper therefore moves from information volume to project shape. A context window may contain a useful source, an obsolete draft, a rejected route, a private note, a public claim, and a warning. If those items are not marked as different kinds of objects, the runtime must infer their status from prose, recency, style, or proximity. That is where coherent misalignment begins. The value of Artificial Tangibility is that it turns context management into object governance. A bounded object is not merely a piece of retrieved text. It carries a declared role. It carries authority status. It carries boundaries. It carries relation to other objects. It may carry an evidence trail. It may carry weight. These fields reduce the runtime's need to guess what the object is allowed to mean. 3. RAG, External Memory, and Source Authority Retrieval-augmented generation and related memory systems establish an important principle: a runtime should not rely only on internal model weights or conversational memory. It should be able to consult external materials. That principle is compatible with Artificial Tangibility. The difference is that retrieval alone does not determine authority. A retrieved document may be relevant and still not govern the current task. It may be historical, superseded, speculative, private, or parked. Artificial Tangibility therefore asks an additional question: once an object is retrieved, what is it allowed to do? This is where source authority becomes central. In a governed project, an object can exist without being promoted. A receipt can prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft can be useful without governing later work. A source can be current in one lane and irrelevant in another. The system must expose those distinctions before the runtime acts. In this sense, Artificial Tangibility is not a replacement for retrieval. It is a governance layer around retrieved and preserved material. It helps determine whether a retrieved object should be trusted, quoted, ignored, archived, used as background, or treated as the active source for the next move. 4. Agent Memory and Externalized Project State Modern agent-memory systems often distinguish working memory, episodic memory, and semantic memory. They do this through databases, vector stores, summaries, thread identifiers, or memory-management policies. Artificial Tangibility expresses a related distinction in plain project terms. A live state board or orientation object functions as working memory: it tells the runtime what is active now. Receipts and communication logs function as episodic memory: they preserve what happened, what changed, what failed, and what remains open. Source-authority objects function as semantic control: they declare which materials govern the present work. The important point is not that files are technically equivalent to databases. They are not. The point is that the human-readable object-world can expose the same categories of state that more technical systems manage implicitly or programmatically. For a solo researcher, small team, or cross-tool workflow, that visibility can be more valuable than hidden sophistication. The method also avoids a common failure in long-running AI work: asking the runtime to remember the project. Artificial Tangibility assumes the runtime is discontinuous. The project must carry continuity outside the runtime so that a future runtime can re-enter without requiring the human to rebuild the whole room. 5. Durable Execution, Re-Entry, and Recoverability Production-grade agent systems often use checkpointers, orchestration engines, and durable execution platforms to recover from crashes, timeouts, rate limits, and incomplete workflows. Those systems persist state so the process can resume. Artificial Tangibility approaches recoverability from the interface side. The question is not only whether a process can resume automatically, but whether a fresh runtime can identify the active object, governing source, unresolved blockers, boundaries, and next safe action. This is the purpose of a re-entry test. A continuity system is working if a runtime can enter from a minimal orientation object and recover the state of the project without relying on the prior chat session. It should be able to answer: What is active? What governs? What is blocked? What must not be touched? What happened last? What should happen next? That test does not replace durable execution in production software systems. It complements it. Durable execution preserves process state. Artificial Tangibility preserves project orientation. In human-AI collaboration, both can matter. 6. Receipts, Provenance, and Failure as Evidence Provenance systems track where information came from, how an artifact was produced, and which activities contributed to its current state. Artificial Tangibility shares this concern through receipts. A receipt is not permission before the work. It is evidence after the work. It records what changed, what was attempted, what remains blocked, and what the next safe action is. In a long-running project, this matters because state drift often occurs silently. A runtime may produce a plausible continuation while using the wrong source, crossing a boundary, or treating draft language as promoted. Receipts make those errors visible. They allow the human and future runtime to ask concrete questions: Was this a source error? An authority error? A boundary error? A state error? A directive error? A missing-evidence error? This is the sense in which failure can become evidence. The goal is not to celebrate mistakes. The goal is to preserve enough telemetry that a mistake can be caught, named, bounded, corrected, and used to strengthen the next handoff. A system that cannot locate its failures cannot safely improve. A system that can name its failures has working edges. 7. In AI systems, this pattern helps reduce coupling, support asynchronous participation, and preserve visible intermediate state. Artificial Tangibility can be understood as a file-based analogue of that pattern. Instead of assuming that each runtime carries the whole project internally, the project maintains a shared state surface: active objects, open items, blockers, receipts, source authority, and next safe actions. The difference again is not that a document is technically the same as a distributed key-value store. It is not. The useful comparison is functional. It also gives humans a place to inspect whether the system is aligned or drifting. For public framing, this matters because it turns a private workflow habit into a recognizable systems pattern. Artificial Tangibility does not ask reviewers to believe in an idiosyncratic folder ritual. It says that shared, inspectable state surfaces are one way to make discontinuous AI collaboration safer and more recoverable. 8. Human-in-the-Loop Governance and Promotion Gates Enterprise AI systems often include human-in-the-loop gates for high-stakes actions. These gates pause execution, require review, and prevent the system from converting uncertain output into authoritative state without oversight. Artificial Tangibility expresses the same governance concern through promotion gates and boundary conditions. A generated artifact can exist without being promoted. A draft can be useful without becoming public. A private constraint can inform the runtime without being leaked into public prose. A source can govern one lane without governing another. The phrase 'existence is not promotion' is central. It prevents a common AI-workflow failure: treating produced text as authorized merely because it has been produced. In a governed project, mutation and promotion are separate events. The runtime may draft, summarize, compare, or propose. The human or declared authority structure determines what becomes canonical, public, or governing. This is not merely a safety preference. It is part of the object grammar. Authority is a field. Boundary is a field. Directive is a field. A runtime that can see those fields can be judged against them. If it crosses them, the error is diagnosable. 9. Object Weight and the Salience Problem The most distinctive contribution of Artificial Tangibility is object weight. Existing systems can store information, retrieve information, trace information, and summarize information. Object weight asks a different question: why does this object matter now? Existence and salience are not the same. A receipt can prove that an object exists. A source map can declare where it belongs. But a runtime may still flatten a hinge object into background if nothing marks its consequence. Weight is the salience layer that tells the runtime not to treat all preserved material equally. Weight can come from consequence, dependency, authority, fragility, risk, or generativity. An object matters if ignoring it would reopen a closed error, corrupt a source hierarchy, erase a breakthrough, or send the project down the wrong path. A weighted object tells the runtime: do not flatten this; read it as a hinge. This is where Artificial Tangibility extends beyond ordinary retrieval or memory. It does not merely ask whether an object can be found. It asks whether the runtime can understand the object's priority inside the current project-world. 10. Those tools solve real technical problems at scale. It also does not claim that Artificial Tangibility invents context engineering, memory, retrieval, provenance, object orientation, affordances, or blackboard coordination. Those are established traditions. The claim is narrower and, for that reason, stronger: long-running AI collaboration needs a human-readable governance layer that binds these concerns together at the level of project work. Artificial Tangibility names that layer. It treats project materials as bounded objects with role, authority, state, boundary, relation, receipt, weight, and next safe action. It tells reviewers how the system can be tested: re-entry speed, source-current distinction, error catchability, safe action selection, handoff quality, stale-context resistance, and preservation of why important objects matter. 11.
