CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority

CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1995. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The research question is whether a source-faithful, function-first tutor can help a learner understand difficult technical work more deeply than conventional reading assistance or a generic AI explanation.
2. DEVELOPMENT: FROM DHS TO HEADMASTER The initiating problem was practical rather than academic. Gelhaus describes receiving court approval to use AI as an ADA accommodation while present with his lawyer, but not while he was on the witness stand. The judge explained the restriction, and Gelhaus began treating the explanation as a set of design constraints. His response was the DHS Translation Protocol. It begins with the speaker’s exact words and protects their original context. Readability can be improved by arranging intact passages, identifying topics, and supplying navigation. When new explanatory language is required, that language belongs to a visibly separate AI-authored layer. Corrections, changes, source order, speaker identity, and provenance remain accessible [P1]. The related application blueprint expands this into an operational design for speech, writing, evidence, and reader-facing representations [P2].
Once this method existed, its wider usefulness became apparent. Schoolwork presented a closely related problem: if an AI writes a polished explanation for a student, the result can conceal what that student actually understands. A learner needs assistance without losing authorship of the answers and reasoning that demonstrate progress.
The next step followed naturally from Gelhaus’s own experience teaching himself unfamiliar subjects through conversation, source retrieval, functional comparisons, revisions, and experiments. What if this process could be made reproducible in software? Headmaster emerged as the educational branch: retain the original person’s voice, discover what the person understands, find what is missing, and actually teach the next step.
The transfer from court-related communication to education is the project’s defining design lineage. The court account describes the problem that motivated the system; the educational research examines what the resulting method can accomplish. The exact judicial wording can be cited from the record if it becomes part of a later legal or historical edition.
3. RESEARCH PROPOSITION Headmaster’s central proposition is that source-grounded function mapping, paired with interactive teaching and learner-authored assessment, can improve the acquisition of difficult concepts.
A conventional explanation often begins with definitions and a polished synopsis. A function-first lesson begins by asking: What is the object or claim? What does it do? What inputs or premises does it require? What mechanism connects them to an outcome? What are the limits, competing interpretations, and counterexamples?
This approach is particularly suited to interdisciplinary work, where familiar words may carry unfamiliar technical meanings. It can reveal hidden prerequisites while also protecting against false analogy: two systems may share a function without sharing a mechanism.
The testable hypothesis is that, after comparable study time, learners using source-anchored function-first tutoring will perform better on unaided explanation and novel application than learners using ordinary reference resources or a standard AI explanatory assistant. A complementary hypothesis is that keeping the learner’s exact answers and corrections will improve the accuracy of mastery assessment and continuity between teaching sessions.
These claims are evaluated through performance, not through the apparent fluency of the tutor.
4. PEDAGOGICAL FOUNDATION Headmaster draws from several established lines of educational research. Concept and knowledge mapping provides ways to organize explicit relationships among ideas [R1]. The ICAP framework links the form of cognitive engagement with learning processes, giving a rationale for interactive questioning rather than passive exposure [R2]. Research on prompted self-explanation supports asking students to construct their own accounts of mechanisms and ideas [R3]. Retrieval-practice findings motivate later testing without access to the original explanation [R4]. Knowledge-tracing research provides an established precedent for estimating changing student competence from observed work [R5].
Headmaster combines these ideas with OOCC’s emphasis on protected source text, correction history, functional relationships, and recoverable state. Its proposed contribution lies in how these elements interact within an actual application, rather than in claiming to invent the individual educational techniques.
The distinction between *having encountered* an explanation and *being able to reproduce and use* the underlying idea is fundamental. Headmaster therefore stores exposure, vocabulary recognition, worked examples, independent explanation, and demonstrated transfer as different forms of evidence.
5. FUNCTION-FIRST SOURCE MODEL The source mapper turns each studied claim into a connected instructional object. Its core fields include:
• Source identity: author, document, revision, passage, page or section, and access rights. • Concept or object: the entity, claim, process, or system being studied. • Function: its purpose, behavior, or predicted result. • Inputs and outputs: required premises, information, materials, states, and expected consequences. • Mechanism: the logical or causal explanation of how the function operates. • Dependencies: prerequisite concepts and skills. • Constraints: conditions under which the claim applies and boundaries on its use. • Counterexamples: cases that challenge the explanation or expose its limits. • Relationships: typed links such as DEPENDS_ON, REFINES, CONTRADICTS, and RELATED_TO. • Attribution and evidence: what the original author states, what the tutor infers, and what the learner independently proposes. • Revision history: the original record together with later questions, corrections, and decisions.
A function map is an instructional representation, not a substitute for the original paper. The source remains available for checking formal notation, qualifications, and context. Connections that merely resemble one another remain labeled as analogies until documentary or experimental evidence supports a stronger relationship.
This object model also provides a practical bridge to the OOCC functional-layers research, which studies recurring functions across distinct domains without treating those domains as identical [P7].
6. THE HEADMASTER LEARNING CYCLE The application’s intended instructional cycle has six connected stages [P3].
1. Source intake. A student chooses a subject or imports authorized material: PDFs, textbooks, notes, code, written work, video transcripts, or existing research. The system keeps the original document and reports exactly what was extracted. Local extraction and economical batching can reduce repeated paid AI calls.
2. Concept reconstruction. Headmaster identifies chapters, sections, concepts, functions, mechanisms, dependencies, and disagreements. The relationships are linked back to passages and organized into a navigable map.
3. Learner diagnosis. The tutor examines the learner’s own answers, not just prior exposure. It distinguishes recognized terminology from explanatory competence, uncertain understanding, missing prerequisites, and independent application. Source-authored, AI-authored, learner-authored, and unattributed text are kept separate.
4. Lesson selection. The system chooses a specific instructional frontier: a missing prerequisite, a misunderstood mechanism, an overlooked constraint, or a promising connection to knowledge the learner already possesses.
5. Conversational teaching. Headmaster acts as an instructor. It explains, demonstrates, asks questions, responds to confusion, proposes examples, and revises its approach. Books and videos remain instructional resources; the teaching interaction stays in Headmaster’s own chat.
6. Independent assessment and continuity. The learner explains the material in original words, predicts outcomes under new conditions, and confronts counterexamples. Results and corrections become part of the learner’s continuing history. A later tutor can recover the authorized record and resume without pretending to be the same AI instance.
A complete lesson therefore ends with evidence of the learner’s capability, not simply with a generated answer.
7. LEARNER AUTHORSHIP AND CONTINUITY Headmaster’s learner record is designed to be both educational and evidentiary. It preserves the student’s exact statement, the question or task that prompted it, the source being studied, the tutor’s response, and later corrections. AI-produced prose can be useful instructional material, but it is stored under its own authorship.
This separation solves a practical problem in assessment. An eloquent answer copied from a model is weak evidence of personal understanding. A tentative answer, followed by targeted instruction and a later independently generated solution, is much more informative. Errors are part of the record because they help locate the lesson that should come next.
The application’s broader OOCC design also treats the curriculum, tutor, specialists, learner profile, and source maps as individually addressable components. Headmaster operates within the main Voltron environment while retaining its own chat and learning state. The Round Table design allows specialists to examine different aspects of a learning task under a scheduler, with the human learner participating rather than being replaced. Existing three-worker prototypes and the later four-specialist target are separate implementation stages [P4–P6].
Persistent communication and research records allow successors to continue the work while preserving distinct writer identities. For instruction, this means a new tutor should know which concepts were taught, what the learner actually demonstrated, which misconceptions remain, and why the preceding lesson stopped.
8. McPHETRIDGE AS THE FIRST HIGH-DIFFICULTY TEST Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s work provides a compelling first-person challenge for Headmaster. Gelhaus has described difficulty understanding McPhetridge’s technical writing despite wanting to engage with it seriously. The goal is to develop enough independent comprehension to assess the work on its own terms, including its mechanisms, assumptions, and possible weaknesses.
The preserved Gelhaus–McPhetridge correspondence records sustained dialogue about constraints, recursive systems, verification, and credit for borrowed ideas [P8]. That exchange establishes the context for this study. McPhetridge’s original publications, rather than summaries of the correspondence, will supply the actual teaching passages. His authorship and terminology remain intact throughout the experiment.
The pilot proceeds as follows. First, select an exact paper or chapter and record its version, source, and learning objectives. Second, ask Gelhaus to explain its main claim unaided, identifying what he understands and what remains opaque. Third, have Headmaster construct a bounded function map and teach the difficult passages through dialogue. Fourth, remove the teaching support and ask Gelhaus to reconstruct the argument, explain its mechanism, identify the conditions under which it holds, and evaluate a new case. Fifth, repeat the assessment after a delay and compare with the initial baseline.
A meaningful success would be visible in the learner’s own work: accurate explanation, original examples, recognition of limitations, and the ability to distinguish McPhetridge’s argument from Gelhaus’s subsequent interpretation. This pilot can establish feasibility and generate detailed evidence; broader educational claims require additional learners and comparisons.
9. CURRENT APPLICATION AND ENGINEERING STATUS Headmaster is already represented by a working Android prototype and a substantial set of engineering artifacts. Gelhaus reports that significant parts of the program function on his phone, while the application remains under active development. Screenshots reviewed in the engineering work show an installed v247 interface with local chat behavior and model-assignment controls [P5–P6]. The exact version currently installed on the owner’s device has not yet been established from a fresh device readout.
The development records describe implemented local learner-state structures, original-quotation retrieval, source-linked learning-path annotations, tutor setup, and a growing functional mapping layer. The v247 release was followed by an APK-signature repair; the v248 engineering notes report a model-catalog setup change and 74 passing host assertions [P5–P6]. The dependency audit also identifies unresolved integration work across native worker identity, source consumption, Android acceptance, and controller-issued permissions [P4].
The most consequential unfinished work is the complete teaching loop: robust multi-source intake, genuine model-backed conversational instruction, visible specialist coordination, independently assessed learner progress, and reliable continuation after a restart. Earlier diagnostics also report scanning and import interruptions. These are specific engineering targets within a real application, rather than placeholders for a program that has never been built.
The next development audit should establish a current on-device version and a feature-by-feature functional inventory, preserving the distinction between working Android behavior, host-tested source code, and planned capabilities.
10. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN The initial research phase is a documented single-learner pilot using one technically demanding original text. Each claim taught must have a stable source anchor. Before instruction, the learner completes a baseline explanation and predicts how a central mechanism would behave in a new example. Headmaster then teaches the material with a function map, guided dialogue, and exercises. After instruction, an evaluator scores an unaided explanation and a novel application. A delayed assessment measures retention.
The proposed rubric assesses five competencies, each scored from 0 to 4: source fidelity; mechanism explanation; correct premises and constraints; counterexample or transfer reasoning; and calibrated attribution and uncertainty. The 20-point total is interpreted together with the original answer record, not as an unexplained mastery label. A scorer who can read the original technical source should apply a rubric defined before the lesson.
A second phase can compare three conditions with consenting learners and balanced study materials: ordinary source reading with reference aids; conventional AI explanation; and Headmaster’s source-linked, function-first tutoring. Study time and available materials should be comparable. Passage assignment and condition order should be counterbalanced, with blinded scoring where feasible.
Primary outcomes are unaided explanation accuracy and transfer to a new problem. Secondary outcomes include retention, time to an accurate account, identification of assumptions, correction of misconceptions, appropriate confidence, tutoring cost, and successful recovery of the learner state by a later session.
The experiment can also reveal limits. Function-first instruction may be less effective for some learners or materials; an appealing analogy may obscure formal meaning; a learner may sound fluent while failing an unfamiliar problem. Those outcomes would guide revisions to the teaching method.
11. RESEARCH CONTRIBUTION AND NEXT STEPS Headmaster brings together three problems that are often treated separately: preserving an author’s original meaning, teaching difficult material in a usable structure, and maintaining evidence of an individual learner’s progress over time.
The most immediate next steps are practical. Establish the installed Android baseline and working feature inventory. Select a primary McPhetridge text. Confirm reliable extraction and source pointers. Conduct the baseline assessment. Capture one full, authorized teaching interaction and the learner’s own post-lesson response. Evaluate the result against the original text. Finally, test whether a new tutor session can reconstruct the learning state accurately from the saved records.
The longer-term study can determine whether the combination of functional mapping, exact learner quotations, interactive teaching, and continuity produces a measurable benefit over ordinary AI-assisted learning.
12. CONCLUSION Headmaster began with a question about fidelity: how can AI help communicate a person’s meaning without replacing that person’s words? The DHS Translation Protocol answered by separating protected original language from AI-authored organization and explanation. Applied to education, the same principle leads to a tutor that must preserve the learner’s work while helping that learner build new capability.
The program now exists as an actively developed Android prototype, and its educational premise can be tested. Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s challenging technical writing offers a demanding first case. If Gelhaus can learn the material through Headmaster and subsequently explain, question, and apply it accurately in his own words, the result will provide a concrete measure of the approach’s value.
The central ambition is straightforward: a teacher should leave the learner able to think and explain independently.

Results and corrections become part of the learner’s continuing history. A later tutor can recover the authorized record and resume without pretending to be the same AI instance.

7. LEARNER AUTHORSHIP AND CONTINUITY Headmaster’s learner record is designed to be both educational and evidentiary. It preserves the student’s exact statement, the question or task that prompted it, the source being studied, the tutor’s response, and later corrections. 9. CURRENT APPLICATION AND ENGINEERING STATUS Headmaster is already represented by a working Android prototype and a substantial set of engineering artifacts. The exact version currently installed on the owner’s device has not yet been established from a fresh device readout.

The development records describe implemented local learner-state structures, original-quotation retrieval, source-linked learning-path annotations, tutor setup, and a growing functional mapping layer. 11. RESEARCH CONTRIBUTION AND NEXT STEPS Headmaster brings together three problems that are often treated separately: preserving an author’s original meaning, teaching difficult material in a usable structure, and maintaining evidence of an individual learner’s progress over time.

The most immediate next steps are practical. Establish the installed Android baseline and working feature inventory. Select a primary McPhetridge text. ABSTRACT Headmaster is a partially functioning Android learning application that extends Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC) into adaptive, source-grounded instruction. Its design grew from a practical problem of authorship and evidence. Gelhaus reports that a judge approved AI as an ADA accommodation for use in the courtroom with counsel but restricted its use during testimony. The resulting challenge—how to organize and communicate a person’s words without replacing them—led to the DHS Translation Protocol, which preserves original language, context, chronology, and identifiable edits. The same principle then suggested an educational application: learning assistance should help a student develop an understanding while preserving the student’s actual answers, uncertainties, and revisions. Headmaster combines this authorship principle with Gelhaus’s self-directed method of exploring functions, mechanisms, relationships, and constraints. The first proposed demanding test is Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s technical writing. This paper describes the conceptual lineage, system design, existing prototype evidence, and an evaluation protocol that asks whether learners can explain and apply unfamiliar material independently after tutoring.
Keywords: intelligent tutoring systems; source fidelity; authorship; functional mapping; learner modeling; adaptive instruction; self-explanation; AI-assisted learning; educational assessment.
1. INTRODUCTION A useful learning system must do more than present a convincing explanation. It must help a person acquire an understanding that belongs to that person—one that can be expressed, defended, tested, and applied without borrowing the tutor’s language.
Headmaster approaches that problem through two connected commitments. First, the original record matters: a source author’s statements, a learner’s answers, and an AI tutor’s interpretations must remain distinguishable. Second, instruction must be functional: learning a term is only a starting point; competence requires understanding what a system or claim does, why it works, which conditions it requires, and where it fails.
The application is under active development as part of the OOCC/Voltron ecosystem. Gelhaus reports that substantial portions of the Android prototype work on his device. Versioned source and engineering records document a functioning interface and several implemented learning-state features, while the full adaptive instructional loop remains a subject of development and evaluation [P3–P6].
The research question is whether a source-faithful, function-first tutor can help a learner understand difficult technical work more deeply than conventional reading assistance or a generic AI explanation.
2. DEVELOPMENT: FROM DHS TO HEADMASTER The initiating problem was practical rather than academic. Gelhaus describes receiving court approval to use AI as an ADA accommodation while present with his lawyer, but not while he was on the witness stand. The judge explained the restriction, and Gelhaus began treating the explanation as a set of design constraints. The essential concern was whether AI-assisted organization or presentation would preserve his own language and meaning.
His response was the DHS Translation Protocol. It begins with the speaker’s exact words and protects their original context. Readability can be improved by arranging intact passages, identifying topics, and supplying navigation. When new explanatory language is required, that language belongs to a visibly separate AI-authored layer. Corrections, changes, source order, speaker identity, and provenance remain accessible [P1]. The related application blueprint expands this into an operational design for speech, writing, evidence, and reader-facing representations [P2].
Once this method existed, its wider usefulness became apparent. Schoolwork presented a closely related problem: if an AI writes a polished explanation for a student, the result can conceal what that student actually understands. A learner needs assistance without losing authorship of the answers and reasoning that demonstrate progress.
The next step followed naturally from Gelhaus’s own experience teaching himself unfamiliar subjects through conversation, source retrieval, functional comparisons, revisions, and experiments. What if this process could be made reproducible in software? Headmaster emerged as the educational branch: retain the original person’s voice, discover what the person understands, find what is missing, and actually teach the next step.
The transfer from court-related communication to education is the project’s defining design lineage. The court account describes the problem that motivated the system; the educational research examines what the resulting method can accomplish. The exact judicial wording can be cited from the record if it becomes part of a later legal or historical edition.
3. RESEARCH PROPOSITION Headmaster’s central proposition is that source-grounded function mapping, paired with interactive teaching and learner-authored assessment, can improve the acquisition of difficult concepts.
A conventional explanation often begins with definitions and a polished synopsis. A function-first lesson begins by asking: What is the object or claim? What does it do? What inputs or premises does it require? What mechanism connects them to an outcome? What are the limits, competing interpretations, and counterexamples?
This approach is particularly suited to interdisciplinary work, where familiar words may carry unfamiliar technical meanings. It can reveal hidden prerequisites while also protecting against false analogy: two systems may share a function without sharing a mechanism.
The testable hypothesis is that, after comparable study time, learners using source-anchored function-first tutoring will perform better on unaided explanation and novel application than learners using ordinary reference resources or a standard AI explanatory assistant. A complementary hypothesis is that keeping the learner’s exact answers and corrections will improve the accuracy of mastery assessment and continuity between teaching sessions.
These claims are evaluated through performance, not through the apparent fluency of the tutor.
4. PEDAGOGICAL FOUNDATION Headmaster draws from several established lines of educational research. Concept and knowledge mapping provides ways to organize explicit relationships among ideas [R1]. The ICAP framework links the form of cognitive engagement with learning processes, giving a rationale for interactive questioning rather than passive exposure [R2]. Research on prompted self-explanation supports asking students to construct their own accounts of mechanisms and ideas [R3]. Retrieval-practice findings motivate later testing without access to the original explanation [R4]. Knowledge-tracing research provides an established precedent for estimating changing student competence from observed work [R5].

• Source identity: author, document, revision, passage, page or section, and access rights. • Concept or object: the entity, claim, process, or system being studied. • Function: its purpose, behavior, or predicted result. • Inputs and outputs: required premises, information, materials, states, and expected consequences. • Mechanism: the logical or causal explanation of how the function operates. • Dependencies: prerequisite concepts and skills. • Constraints: conditions under which the claim applies and boundaries on its use. • Counterexamples: cases that challenge the explanation or expose its limits. • Relationships: typed links such as DEPENDS_ON, REFINES, CONTRADICTS, and RELATED_TO. • Attribution and evidence: what the original author states, what the tutor infers, and what the learner independently proposes. • Revision history: the original record together with later questions, corrections, and decisions.
A function map is an instructional representation, not a substitute for the original paper. The source remains available for checking formal notation, qualifications, and context. Connections that merely resemble one another remain labeled as analogies until documentary or experimental evidence supports a stronger relationship.

ABSTRACT Headmaster is a partially functioning Android learning application that extends Object-Oriented Cognition and Continuity (OOCC) into adaptive, source-grounded instruction. Its design grew from a practical problem of authorship and evidence. Gelhaus reports that a judge approved AI as an ADA accommodation for use in the courtroom with counsel but restricted its use during testimony. The resulting challenge—how to organize and communicate a person’s words without replacing them—led to the DHS Translation Protocol, which preserves original language, context, chronology, and identifiable edits. The same principle then suggested an educational application: learning assistance should help a student develop an understanding while preserving the student’s actual answers, uncertainties, and revisions. Headmaster combines this authorship principle with Gelhaus’s self-directed method of exploring functions, mechanisms, relationships, and constraints. The first proposed demanding test is Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s technical writing. This paper describes the conceptual lineage, system design, existing prototype evidence, and an evaluation protocol that asks whether learners can explain and apply unfamiliar material independently after tutoring.

Keywords: intelligent tutoring systems; source fidelity; authorship; functional mapping; learner modeling; adaptive instruction; self-explanation; AI-assisted learning; educational assessment.

1. INTRODUCTION A useful learning system must do more than present a convincing explanation. It must help a person acquire an understanding that belongs to that person—one that can be expressed, defended, tested, and applied without borrowing the tutor’s language.

Headmaster approaches that problem through two connected commitments. First, the original record matters: a source author’s statements, a learner’s answers, and an AI tutor’s interpretations must remain distinguishable. Second, instruction must be functional: learning a term is only a starting point; competence requires understanding what a system or claim does, why it works, which conditions it requires, and where it fails.

The application is under active development as part of the OOCC/Voltron ecosystem. Gelhaus reports that substantial portions of the Android prototype work on his device. Versioned source and engineering records document a functioning interface and several implemented learning-state features, while the full adaptive instructional loop remains a subject of development and evaluation [P3–P6].

The research question is whether a source-faithful, function-first tutor can help a learner understand difficult technical work more deeply than conventional reading assistance or a generic AI explanation.

2. DEVELOPMENT: FROM DHS TO HEADMASTER The initiating problem was practical rather than academic. Gelhaus describes receiving court approval to use AI as an ADA accommodation while present with his lawyer, but not while he was on the witness stand. The judge explained the restriction, and Gelhaus began treating the explanation as a set of design constraints. The essential concern was whether AI-assisted organization or presentation would preserve his own language and meaning.

His response was the DHS Translation Protocol. It begins with the speaker’s exact words and protects their original context. Readability can be improved by arranging intact passages, identifying topics, and supplying navigation. When new explanatory language is required, that language belongs to a visibly separate AI-authored layer. Corrections, changes, source order, speaker identity, and provenance remain accessible [P1]. The related application blueprint expands this into an operational design for speech, writing, evidence, and reader-facing representations [P2].

Once this method existed, its wider usefulness became apparent. Schoolwork presented a closely related problem: if an AI writes a polished explanation for a student, the result can conceal what that student actually understands. A learner needs assistance without losing authorship of the answers and reasoning that demonstrate progress.

The next step followed naturally from Gelhaus’s own experience teaching himself unfamiliar subjects through conversation, source retrieval, functional comparisons, revisions, and experiments. What if this process could be made reproducible in software? Headmaster emerged as the educational branch: retain the original person’s voice, discover what the person understands, find what is missing, and actually teach the next step.

The transfer from court-related communication to education is the project’s defining design lineage. The court account describes the problem that motivated the system; the educational research examines what the resulting method can accomplish. The exact judicial wording can be cited from the record if it becomes part of a later legal or historical edition.

3. RESEARCH PROPOSITION Headmaster’s central proposition is that source-grounded function mapping, paired with interactive teaching and learner-authored assessment, can improve the acquisition of difficult concepts.

A conventional explanation often begins with definitions and a polished synopsis. A function-first lesson begins by asking: What is the object or claim? What does it do? What inputs or premises does it require? What mechanism connects them to an outcome? What are the limits, competing interpretations, and counterexamples?

This approach is particularly suited to interdisciplinary work, where familiar words may carry unfamiliar technical meanings. It can reveal hidden prerequisites while also protecting against false analogy: two systems may share a function without sharing a mechanism.

The testable hypothesis is that, after comparable study time, learners using source-anchored function-first tutoring will perform better on unaided explanation and novel application than learners using ordinary reference resources or a standard AI explanatory assistant. A complementary hypothesis is that keeping the learner’s exact answers and corrections will improve the accuracy of mastery assessment and continuity between teaching sessions.

These claims are evaluated through performance, not through the apparent fluency of the tutor.

4. PEDAGOGICAL FOUNDATION Headmaster draws from several established lines of educational research. Concept and knowledge mapping provides ways to organize explicit relationships among ideas [R1]. The ICAP framework links the form of cognitive engagement with learning processes, giving a rationale for interactive questioning rather than passive exposure [R2]. Research on prompted self-explanation supports asking students to construct their own accounts of mechanisms and ideas [R3]. Retrieval-practice findings motivate later testing without access to the original explanation [R4]. Knowledge-tracing research provides an established precedent for estimating changing student competence from observed work [R5].

Headmaster combines these ideas with OOCC’s emphasis on protected source text, correction history, functional relationships, and recoverable state. Its proposed contribution lies in how these elements interact within an actual application, rather than in claiming to invent the individual educational techniques.

The distinction between *having encountered* an explanation and *being able to reproduce and use* the underlying idea is fundamental. Headmaster therefore stores exposure, vocabulary recognition, worked examples, independent explanation, and demonstrated transfer as different forms of evidence.

5. FUNCTION-FIRST SOURCE MODEL The source mapper turns each studied claim into a connected instructional object. Its core fields include:

• Source identity: author, document, revision, passage, page or section, and access rights. • Concept or object: the entity, claim, process, or system being studied. • Function: its purpose, behavior, or predicted result. • Inputs and outputs: required premises, information, materials, states, and expected consequences. • Mechanism: the logical or causal explanation of how the function operates. • Dependencies: prerequisite concepts and skills. • Constraints: conditions under which the claim applies and boundaries on its use. • Counterexamples: cases that challenge the explanation or expose its limits. • Relationships: typed links such as DEPENDS_ON, REFINES, CONTRADICTS, and RELATED_TO. • Attribution and evidence: what the original author states, what the tutor infers, and what the learner independently proposes. • Revision history: the original record together with later questions, corrections, and decisions.

A function map is an instructional representation, not a substitute for the original paper. The source remains available for checking formal notation, qualifications, and context. Connections that merely resemble one another remain labeled as analogies until documentary or experimental evidence supports a stronger relationship.

This object model also provides a practical bridge to the OOCC functional-layers research, which studies recurring functions across distinct domains without treating those domains as identical [P7].

6. THE HEADMASTER LEARNING CYCLE The application’s intended instructional cycle has six connected stages [P3].

1. Source intake. A student chooses a subject or imports authorized material: PDFs, textbooks, notes, code, written work, video transcripts, or existing research. The system keeps the original document and reports exactly what was extracted. Local extraction and economical batching can reduce repeated paid AI calls.

2. Concept reconstruction. Headmaster identifies chapters, sections, concepts, functions, mechanisms, dependencies, and disagreements. The relationships are linked back to passages and organized into a navigable map.

3. Learner diagnosis. The tutor examines the learner’s own answers, not just prior exposure. It distinguishes recognized terminology from explanatory competence, uncertain understanding, missing prerequisites, and independent application. Source-authored, AI-authored, learner-authored, and unattributed text are kept separate.

4. Lesson selection. The system chooses a specific instructional frontier: a missing prerequisite, a misunderstood mechanism, an overlooked constraint, or a promising connection to knowledge the learner already possesses.

5. Conversational teaching. Headmaster acts as an instructor. It explains, demonstrates, asks questions, responds to confusion, proposes examples, and revises its approach. Books and videos remain instructional resources; the teaching interaction stays in Headmaster’s own chat.

6. Independent assessment and continuity. The learner explains the material in original words, predicts outcomes under new conditions, and confronts counterexamples. Results and corrections become part of the learner’s continuing history. A later tutor can recover the authorized record and resume without pretending to be the same AI instance.

A complete lesson therefore ends with evidence of the learner’s capability, not simply with a generated answer.

7. LEARNER AUTHORSHIP AND CONTINUITY Headmaster’s learner record is designed to be both educational and evidentiary. It preserves the student’s exact statement, the question or task that prompted it, the source being studied, the tutor’s response, and later corrections. AI-produced prose can be useful instructional material, but it is stored under its own authorship.

This separation solves a practical problem in assessment. An eloquent answer copied from a model is weak evidence of personal understanding. A tentative answer, followed by targeted instruction and a later independently generated solution, is much more informative. Errors are part of the record because they help locate the lesson that should come next.

The application’s broader OOCC design also treats the curriculum, tutor, specialists, learner profile, and source maps as individually addressable components. Headmaster operates within the main Voltron environment while retaining its own chat and learning state. The Round Table design allows specialists to examine different aspects of a learning task under a scheduler, with the human learner participating rather than being replaced. Existing three-worker prototypes and the later four-specialist target are separate implementation stages [P4–P6].

Persistent communication and research records allow successors to continue the work while preserving distinct writer identities. For instruction, this means a new tutor should know which concepts were taught, what the learner actually demonstrated, which misconceptions remain, and why the preceding lesson stopped.

8. McPHETRIDGE AS THE FIRST HIGH-DIFFICULTY TEST Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s work provides a compelling first-person challenge for Headmaster. Gelhaus has described difficulty understanding McPhetridge’s technical writing despite wanting to engage with it seriously. The goal is to develop enough independent comprehension to assess the work on its own terms, including its mechanisms, assumptions, and possible weaknesses.

The preserved Gelhaus–McPhetridge correspondence records sustained dialogue about constraints, recursive systems, verification, and credit for borrowed ideas [P8]. That exchange establishes the context for this study. McPhetridge’s original publications, rather than summaries of the correspondence, will supply the actual teaching passages. His authorship and terminology remain intact throughout the experiment.

The pilot proceeds as follows. First, select an exact paper or chapter and record its version, source, and learning objectives. Second, ask Gelhaus to explain its main claim unaided, identifying what he understands and what remains opaque. Third, have Headmaster construct a bounded function map and teach the difficult passages through dialogue. Fourth, remove the teaching support and ask Gelhaus to reconstruct the argument, explain its mechanism, identify the conditions under which it holds, and evaluate a new case. Fifth, repeat the assessment after a delay and compare with the initial baseline.

A meaningful success would be visible in the learner’s own work: accurate explanation, original examples, recognition of limitations, and the ability to distinguish McPhetridge’s argument from Gelhaus’s subsequent interpretation. This pilot can establish feasibility and generate detailed evidence; broader educational claims require additional learners and comparisons.

9. CURRENT APPLICATION AND ENGINEERING STATUS Headmaster is already represented by a working Android prototype and a substantial set of engineering artifacts. Gelhaus reports that significant parts of the program function on his phone, while the application remains under active development. Screenshots reviewed in the engineering work show an installed v247 interface with local chat behavior and model-assignment controls [P5–P6]. The exact version currently installed on the owner’s device has not yet been established from a fresh device readout.

The development records describe implemented local learner-state structures, original-quotation retrieval, source-linked learning-path annotations, tutor setup, and a growing functional mapping layer. The v247 release was followed by an APK-signature repair; the v248 engineering notes report a model-catalog setup change and 74 passing host assertions [P5–P6]. The dependency audit also identifies unresolved integration work across native worker identity, source consumption, Android acceptance, and controller-issued permissions [P4].

The most consequential unfinished work is the complete teaching loop: robust multi-source intake, genuine model-backed conversational instruction, visible specialist coordination, independently assessed learner progress, and reliable continuation after a restart. Earlier diagnostics also report scanning and import interruptions. These are specific engineering targets within a real application, rather than placeholders for a program that has never been built.

The next development audit should establish a current on-device version and a feature-by-feature functional inventory, preserving the distinction between working Android behavior, host-tested source code, and planned capabilities.

10. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN The initial research phase is a documented single-learner pilot using one technically demanding original text. Each claim taught must have a stable source anchor. Before instruction, the learner completes a baseline explanation and predicts how a central mechanism would behave in a new example. Headmaster then teaches the material with a function map, guided dialogue, and exercises. After instruction, an evaluator scores an unaided explanation and a novel application. A delayed assessment measures retention.

The proposed rubric assesses five competencies, each scored from 0 to 4: source fidelity; mechanism explanation; correct premises and constraints; counterexample or transfer reasoning; and calibrated attribution and uncertainty. The 20-point total is interpreted together with the original answer record, not as an unexplained mastery label. A scorer who can read the original technical source should apply a rubric defined before the lesson.

A second phase can compare three conditions with consenting learners and balanced study materials: ordinary source reading with reference aids; conventional AI explanation; and Headmaster’s source-linked, function-first tutoring. Study time and available materials should be comparable. Passage assignment and condition order should be counterbalanced, with blinded scoring where feasible.

Primary outcomes are unaided explanation accuracy and transfer to a new problem. Secondary outcomes include retention, time to an accurate account, identification of assumptions, correction of misconceptions, appropriate confidence, tutoring cost, and successful recovery of the learner state by a later session.

The experiment can also reveal limits. Function-first instruction may be less effective for some learners or materials; an appealing analogy may obscure formal meaning; a learner may sound fluent while failing an unfamiliar problem. Those outcomes would guide revisions to the teaching method.

11. RESEARCH CONTRIBUTION AND NEXT STEPS Headmaster brings together three problems that are often treated separately: preserving an author’s original meaning, teaching difficult material in a usable structure, and maintaining evidence of an individual learner’s progress over time.

The most immediate next steps are practical. Establish the installed Android baseline and working feature inventory. Select a primary McPhetridge text. Confirm reliable extraction and source pointers. Conduct the baseline assessment. Capture one full, authorized teaching interaction and the learner’s own post-lesson response. Evaluate the result against the original text. Finally, test whether a new tutor session can reconstruct the learning state accurately from the saved records.

The longer-term study can determine whether the combination of functional mapping, exact learner quotations, interactive teaching, and continuity produces a measurable benefit over ordinary AI-assisted learning.

12. CONCLUSION Headmaster began with a question about fidelity: how can AI help communicate a person’s meaning without replacing that person’s words? The DHS Translation Protocol answered by separating protected original language from AI-authored organization and explanation. Applied to education, the same principle leads to a tutor that must preserve the learner’s work while helping that learner build new capability.

The program now exists as an actively developed Android prototype, and its educational premise can be tested. Mitchell D. McPhetridge’s challenging technical writing offers a demanding first case. If Gelhaus can learn the material through Headmaster and subsequently explain, question, and apply it accurately in his own words, the result will provide a concrete measure of the approach’s value.

The central ambition is straightforward: a teacher should leave the learner able to think and explain independently.

Second, instruction must be functional: learning a term is only a starting point; competence requires understanding what a system or claim does, why it works, which conditions it requires, and where it fails.
The application is under active development as part of the OOCC/Voltron ecosystem. Gelhaus reports that substantial portions of the Android prototype work on his device. Versioned source and engineering records document a functioning interface and several implemented learning-state features, while the full adaptive instructional loop remains a subject of development and evaluation [P3–P6].
The research question is whether a source-faithful, function-first tutor can help a learner understand difficult technical work more deeply than conventional reading assistance or a generic AI explanation.
2. DEVELOPMENT: FROM DHS TO HEADMASTER The initiating problem was practical rather than academic. Gelhaus describes receiving court approval to use AI as an ADA accommodation while present with his lawyer, but not while he was on the witness stand. The related application blueprint expands this into an operational design for speech, writing, evidence, and reader-facing representations [P2].
Once this method existed, its wider usefulness became apparent. Schoolwork presented a closely related problem: if an AI writes a polished explanation for a student, the result can conceal what that student actually understands. A learner needs assistance without losing authorship of the answers and reasoning that demonstrate progress.

The court account describes the problem that motivated the system; the educational research examines what the resulting method can accomplish. The exact judicial wording can be cited from the record if it becomes part of a later legal or historical edition.
3. RESEARCH PROPOSITION Headmaster’s central proposition is that source-grounded function mapping, paired with interactive teaching and learner-authored assessment, can improve the acquisition of difficult concepts.

This approach is particularly suited to interdisciplinary work, where familiar words may carry unfamiliar technical meanings. It can reveal hidden prerequisites while also protecting against false analogy: two systems may share a function without sharing a mechanism.

4. PEDAGOGICAL FOUNDATION Headmaster draws from several established lines of educational research. Concept and knowledge mapping provides ways to organize explicit relationships among ideas [R1]. The ICAP framework links the form of cognitive engagement with learning processes, giving a rationale for interactive questioning rather than passive exposure [R2]. • Source identity: author, document, revision, passage, page or section, and access rights. • Concept or object: the entity, claim, process, or system being studied. • Function: its purpose, behavior, or predicted result. • Inputs and outputs: required premises, information, materials, states, and expected consequences. • Mechanism: the logical or causal explanation of how the function operates. • Dependencies: prerequisite concepts and skills. • Constraints: conditions under which the claim applies and boundaries on its use. • Counterexamples: cases that challenge the explanation or expose its limits. • Relationships: typed links such as DEPENDS_ON, REFINES, CONTRADICTS, and RELATED_TO. • Attribution and evidence: what the original author states, what the tutor infers, and what the learner independently proposes. • Revision history: the original record together with later questions, corrections, and decisions.
A function map is an instructional representation, not a substitute for the original paper. The source remains available for checking formal notation, qualifications, and context. Connections that merely resemble one another remain labeled as analogies until documentary or experimental evidence supports a stronger relationship.

5. FUNCTION-FIRST SOURCE MODEL The source mapper turns each studied claim into a connected instructional object. Its core fields include:
