CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority

CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. References Clark, Andy, and David J. Chalmers. “The Extended Mind.” Analysis 58, no. 1 (1998): 7-19. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility: Why Object Orientation Works for AI Runtimes.” Manuscript, 2026a. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management.” Manuscript, 2026b. Hutchins, Edwin. Cognition in the Wild. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1995. Liu, Nelson F., Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, and Percy Liang. “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2307.03172 (2023); Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024). Norman, Donald A. The Design of Everyday Things. Revised and Expanded Edition. New York: Basic Books, 2013. World Wide Web Consortium. Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2. W3C Recommendation, June 6, 2023. Yao, Shunyu, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, and Yuan Cao. “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.03629 (2022).

Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. candidates.body_html:
Canonical Tokens A Minimal Representatio

Canonical Tokens Canonical Tokens: A Minimal-Representation Principle for AI-Assisted Continuity Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract AI-assisted continuity work spends real, avoidable cost re-explaining references that are already at their minimal possible form. A number does not become more precise by being spelled out in longer language; it is already its own shortest correct description. An established name, once assigned, carries its referent without needing to be redefined at each use. This paper proposes the canonical token principle: certain references - numbers, assigned names, and fixed coordinate handles - should be treated as representationally complete once established, and re-expanding them in later context is waste rather than clarity. The paper grounds this claim in algorithmic information theory, where the shortest correct description of an object is a well- defined and long-studied quantity, and extends it into AI-assisted project work through the Authority concept already proposed in Continuity, Authority, Directive. It also confronts a genuine complication directly: current large language model tokenizers do not reliably treat numbers as stable, canonical units internally, which produces measurable arithmetic errors. This paper’s claim operates at a different layer - the documentation and prompting layer, not the tokenizer’s internal representation - and the paper is explicit about that boundary rather than overstating what it fixes. Keywords: AI continuity, minimum description length, Kolmogorov complexity, canonical representation, tokenization, context efficiency, AI state management, object-oriented cognition This is the fourth paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) proposes that bounded objects give non-embodied AI runtimes operational grip. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that proposal against existing AI state-management patterns. Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposes a control grammar for governing those objects. This paper narrows further, to a single governance question those earlier papers assume but do not resolve: once a reference is established, when should it ever need to be re-explained? 1. The Problem: Re-Explaining What Is Already Minimal Long-running AI-assisted work regularly wastes effort re-describing things that cannot be described more efficiently than they already are. A number is the clearest case. Three is already three. There is no shorter, more precise way to refer to the quantity three than the token that already means three. Spelling out “the third item in the sequence” instead of writing “3” does not add precision. It adds length without adding information. A name behaves the same way once it is assigned. If a person, object, or coordinate has been given a stable name, that name is already a complete, minimal reference to the thing it names. Re-explaining who or what the name refers to every time it appears is not caution. It is redundant expansion of something that was already at its shortest correct form. This matters more in AI-assisted work than it might first appear, for a reason specific to how these systems operate. Every re-explanation is not free. It occupies context, competes with other material for the runtime’s attention, and in genuinely long or multi-document work, contributes directly to the same context-without-shape problem described elsewhere in this sequence (Gelhaus, 2026a, 2026b). A project that repeatedly re-spells-out numbers, re-defines established names, or re-explains fixed coordinates is paying a real, cumulative cost for information that did not need to be resupplied. The claim of this paper is narrow and specific: certain references are already canonical. Once established, they should be treated as complete, not as invitations to re-explain. 2. Canonical Form Has a Real, Existing Definition This is not a new idea invented for AI-assisted work. It has a name and a long history in information theory: the shortest correct description of an object, below which no further compression is possible without losing information, is formalized as Kolmogorov complexity, introduced as one of three approaches to a quantitative definition of information (Kolmogorov, 1965). A number’s own digit representation is at or near this floor for the overwhelming majority of practical purposes - there is no shorter correct way to specify the number 3 than a token that means 3. The related Minimum Description Length principle extends this from individual objects to entire models: the best description of a body of data is the one that minimizes the combined length of the model and the data described through it (Rissanen, 1978). Applied to project documentation rather than statistical modeling, the same logic holds: the best record of a project state is not the one that repeats the most detail, but the one that encodes established references at their minimal form and spends its remaining length on what is actually new. This grounding matters because it keeps the claim honest and bounded. This paper is not arguing that shorter is always better, or that all context should be compressed indiscriminately. It is arguing something much narrower: a specific, well-defined class of references - fixed numbers, assigned names, established coordinate handles - are already at or near their representational floor, and treating them as if they need further unpacking is a documented, named category of waste, not a stylistic preference. 3. Canonical Tokens as an Authority State Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposed Authority as the field that tells a runtime what a given object’s status is: current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted. This paper proposes that canonical tokens deserve their own authority state, distinct from the others: established and complete. An object with this status is not a draft awaiting revision, nor a source awaiting promotion. It is a reference that has already reached its minimal correct form and requires no further processing to be trusted. A number is established and complete the moment it is written. A name is established and complete the moment it is assigned and recorded once, in an index or reference list, the same way a receipt or Blackboard already functions elsewhere in this sequence. This has a direct practical consequence for AI-assisted work: once a runtime has seen a canonical token defined - a name assigned to a person, a coordinate assigned to an object, a number stated in context - it should treat later appearances of that same token as already resolved, not as an occasion to redefine, re-describe, or expand. The correct action on encountering an established canonical token again is to use it, not to re-explain it. This is consistent with, and a direct extension of, a rule already present informally in this project’s own working practice: a short, stable handle carries the reference, while the meaning of that handle lives once, in an index, rather than being repeated at every point of use. What this paper adds is the theoretical grounding for why that rule works - not merely as a convenient habit, but as an application of a well- established, decades-old principle about the floor of correct description. 4. A Genuine Complication: Tokenizers Do Not Yet Honor This Principle Internally Any paper making a claim this clean about numbers deserves to be tested against what actually happens inside the systems it is written for. The honest answer is that current large language model tokenizers do not reliably treat numbers as stable, canonical units at all. Standard byte-pair-encoding tokenizers frequently split numbers inconsistently: one three-digit number may be represented as a single token while a neighboring three- digit number is split across two or three tokens, depending on how frequently that specific digit sequence appeared during training rather than on any property of the number itself (Singh and Strouse, 2024). This is not a minor cosmetic issue. The same research demonstrates that this inconsistency produces measurable, stereotyped arithmetic errors, and that changing the tokenization direction or forcing consistent digit grouping (for example, by inserting separators) measurably improves accuracy. This is a real complication, and it should not be minimized or explained away. It means that at the level of the model’s internal representation, the number 3 and the number 703 are not treated with the same kind of canonical stability this paper is arguing for at the documentation layer. The floor this paper describes is a property of the number itself, in principle; it is not yet a property reliably respected by the tokenizer that turns that number into the units a model actually computes over. The honest resolution is to be precise about which layer this paper’s claim operates on. This paper is not a claim about tokenizer design, and it does not propose a fix for inconsistent internal digit segmentation. It is a claim about the documentation and prompting layer: how humans and AI-assisted systems should treat already- established references in the text of a project - project notes, handoff files, receipts, source maps - regardless of how a given tokenizer happens to segment that text internally. A canonical token, once established in a project’s documentation, should not be re-expanded in later prose even if the model’s own tokenizer is, at a lower level, still doing something less clean with the underlying digits. The two problems are related in spirit - both are about respecting a stable, minimal representation - but they are not the same problem, and this paper does not claim to solve both. 5. The Practical Rule The operational rule this paper proposes is simple to state and directly testable: establish a canonical token once, in an index or reference object, and treat every later appearance of that same token as already resolved. For numbers, this means not re-deriving or re-explaining a quantity once it has been stated - referring back to it directly rather than restating its derivation or spelling it out in longer language. For names, this means assigning a name once, recording what it refers to in a single place, and using the bare name afterward rather than re-describing the referent at each use. For coordinate handles - the short, machine-facing identifiers used elsewhere in this sequence to name objects, lanes, and receipts - this means treating the handle itself as the canonical reference, with its meaning living once in an index rather than being re-explained inline every time the handle is used. The failure mode this rule prevents is cumulative rather than dramatic. No single re- explanation of an established token is very costly. But a project that habitually re- derives, re-describes, or re-spells-out already-established references pays that cost repeatedly, and in long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime work, that repeated cost is exactly the kind of unstructured burden the rest of this sequence has already argued against (Gelhaus, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c). 6. Boundary Conditions and Limits This principle applies specifically to references that are genuinely already minimal: fixed numbers, assigned names, and established coordinate handles. It does not apply to descriptions, arguments, or explanations, which frequently do benefit from restatement, elaboration, or repetition for clarity. The claim is narrow on purpose. This paper also does not claim to resolve the tokenizer-level inconsistency documented in Section 4. That is a model-architecture and training-data problem, addressed by a separate and active line of research, not by project documentation discipline. Finally, this principle depends on the canonical token actually having been established clearly before it is reused. If a name or handle is introduced ambiguously, or if the same handle is later reused for a different referent, the principle breaks down - not because the principle is wrong, but because its precondition, a genuinely established and complete reference, was never actually met. This is the same kind of dependency on disciplined use already acknowledged for Continuity, Authority, and Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c): the grammar only works if the objects it governs are maintained honestly. 7. Evaluation Criteria This claim should be testable rather than merely plausible. Four criteria are proposed. First, context economy: a project that establishes canonical tokens once and reuses them without re-expansion should require measurably less context to convey the same information than one that re-explains established references repeatedly. Second, reduced drift: a runtime working from a project with clearly established canonical tokens should be less likely to introduce inconsistent restatements of the same number or name across a long document or a long multi-session project. Third, faster verification: a human reviewing project output should be able to check an established token against its single index entry more quickly than reconstructing its meaning from repeated, possibly slightly inconsistent, restatements scattered through the text. Fourth, clean failure: when a canonical token is misused - reused for a different referent, or contradicted by a later restatement - that failure should be easy to locate precisely because the correct behavior (use the established token without re- expansion) is simple and specific enough that a violation stands out clearly. 8. Conclusion Some references are already as short as they can correctly be. A number is its own minimal description. An assigned name, once recorded, is a complete reference to what it names. Treating these as things that must be re-explained on every appearance is not thoroughness. It is the accumulation of avoidable cost in exactly the kind of long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime AI-assisted work this sequence has been concerned with throughout. This paper grounds that observation in an existing, well-established idea - the floor of correct description, formalized decades ago in algorithmic information theory - rather than presenting it as a new invention. It extends Continuity, Authority, Directive by proposing a specific authority state for canonical tokens: established and complete, requiring no further processing once recorded. And it confronts, rather than avoids, the genuine complication that current tokenizers do not yet honor this principle at the level of internal model representation, drawing a clear boundary between what this paper’s discipline actually governs and what remains a separate, open research problem. The practical instruction is simple: name it once, record what it means once, and afterward, use the name. References Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility: Why Object Orientation Works for AI Runtimes.” Manuscript, 2026a. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management.” Manuscript, 2026b. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work.” Manuscript, 2026c. Kolmogorov, Andrei N. “Three Approaches to the Quantitative Definition of Information.” Problems of Information Transmission 1, no. 1 (1965): 1-7. Rissanen, Jorma. “Modeling by Shortest Data Description.” Automatica 14, no. 5 (1978): 465-471. Singh, Aaditya K., and DJ Strouse. “Tokenization Counts: The Impact of Tokenization on Arithmetic in Frontier LLMs.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2402.14903 (2024).

The same research demonstrates that this inconsistency produces measurable, stereotyped arithmetic errors, and that changing the tokenization direction or forcing consistent digit grouping (for example, by inserting separators) measurably improves accuracy. This is a real complication, and it should not be minimized or explained away. It means that at the level of the model’s internal representation, the number 3 and the number 703 are not treated with the same kind of canonical stability this paper is arguing for at the documentation layer. The floor this paper describes is a property of the number itself, in principle; it is not yet a property reliably respected by the tokenizer that turns that number into the units a model actually computes over. The honest resolution is to be precise about which layer this paper’s claim operates on. This paper is not a claim about tokenizer design, and it does not propose a fix for inconsistent internal digit segmentation. It is a claim about the documentation and prompting layer: how humans and AI-assisted systems should treat already- established references in the text of a project - project notes, handoff files, receipts, source maps - regardless of how a given tokenizer happens to segment that text internally. A canonical token, once established in a project’s documentation, should not be re-expanded in later prose even if the model’s own tokenizer is, at a lower level, still doing something less clean with the underlying digits. The two problems are related in spirit - both are about respecting a stable, minimal representation - but they are not the same problem, and this paper does not claim to solve both. 5. The Practical Rule The operational rule this paper proposes is simple to state and directly testable: establish a canonical token once, in an index or reference object, and treat every later appearance of that same token as already resolved. For numbers, this means not re-deriving or re-explaining a quantity once it has been stated - referring back to it directly rather than restating its derivation or spelling it out in longer language. For names, this means assigning a name once, recording what it refers to in a single place, and using the bare name afterward rather than re-describing the referent at each use. For coordinate handles - the short, machine-facing identifiers used elsewhere in this sequence to name objects, lanes, and receipts - this means treating the handle itself as the canonical reference, with its meaning living once in an index rather than being re-explained inline every time the handle is used. The failure mode this rule prevents is cumulative rather than dramatic. No single re- explanation of an established token is very costly. But a project that habitually re- derives, re-describes, or re-spells-out already-established references pays that cost repeatedly, and in long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime work, that repeated cost is exactly the kind of unstructured burden the rest of this sequence has already argued against (Gelhaus, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c). 6. Boundary Conditions and Limits This principle applies specifically to references that are genuinely already minimal: fixed numbers, assigned names, and established coordinate handles. It does not apply to descriptions, arguments, or explanations, which frequently do benefit from restatement, elaboration, or repetition for clarity. The claim is narrow on purpose. This paper also does not claim to resolve the tokenizer-level inconsistency documented in Section 4. That is a model-architecture and training-data problem, addressed by a separate and active line of research, not by project documentation discipline. Finally, this principle depends on the canonical token actually having been established clearly before it is reused. If a name or handle is introduced ambiguously, or if the same handle is later reused for a different referent, the principle breaks down - not because the principle is wrong, but because its precondition, a genuinely established and complete reference, was never actually met. This is the same kind of dependency on disciplined use already acknowledged for Continuity, Authority, and Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c): the grammar only works if the objects it governs are maintained honestly. 7. Evaluation Criteria This claim should be testable rather than merely plausible. Four criteria are proposed. First, context economy: a project that establishes canonical tokens once and reuses them without re-expansion should require measurably less context to convey the same information than one that re-explains established references repeatedly. Second, reduced drift: a runtime working from a project with clearly established canonical tokens should be less likely to introduce inconsistent restatements of the same number or name across a long document or a long multi-session project. Third, faster verification: a human reviewing project output should be able to check an established token against its single index entry more quickly than reconstructing its meaning from repeated, possibly slightly inconsistent, restatements scattered through the text. Fourth, clean failure: when a canonical token is misused - reused for a different referent, or contradicted by a later restatement - that failure should be easy to locate precisely because the correct behavior (use the established token without re- expansion) is simple and specific enough that a violation stands out clearly. 8. Conclusion Some references are already as short as they can correctly be. A number is its own minimal description. An assigned name, once recorded, is a complete reference to what it names. Treating these as things that must be re-explained on every appearance is not thoroughness. It is the accumulation of avoidable cost in exactly the kind of long-running, multi-document, multi-runtime AI-assisted work this sequence has been concerned with throughout. This paper grounds that observation in an existing, well-established idea - the floor of correct description, formalized decades ago in algorithmic information theory - rather than presenting it as a new invention. It extends Continuity, Authority, Directive by proposing a specific authority state for canonical tokens: established and complete, requiring no further processing once recorded. And it confronts, rather than avoids, the genuine complication that current tokenizers do not yet honor this principle at the level of internal model representation, drawing a clear boundary between what this paper’s discipline actually governs and what remains a separate, open research problem. The practical instruction is simple: name it once, record what it means once, and afterward, use the name. References Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility: Why Object Orientation Works for AI Runtimes.” Manuscript, 2026a. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Artificial Tangibility as a Low-Infrastructure Governance Layer for AI State Management.” Manuscript, 2026b. Gelhaus, Benjamin. “Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work.” Manuscript, 2026c. Rissanen, Jorma. “Modeling by Shortest Data Description.” Automatica 14, no. 5 (1978): 465-471.
