The Object as Filter The Object as Filter: Holographic Return, AI Continuity, and Human-Readable Interfaces Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract This paper argues that a single structural pattern recurs across three domains usually treated as unrelated: biological perception, the foundations-of-physics debate over observation and reality, and AI-facing continuity architecture. In each domain, an overwhelming, undifferentiated field is made navigable not by receiving it in full, but by filtering it into bounded, action-relevant units. Perceptual interface theory argues that organisms do not perceive reality directly but through a fitness-tuned interface that discards nearly all available information. A body of foundational- physics work, most notably John Wheeler’s participatory universe proposal, has speculated that observation itself may be constitutive of legible physical reality rather than a passive report on a reality that already existed in full. Object-oriented AI continuity architecture, developed across a companion sequence of papers, argues that AI runtimes require bounded, authority-marked, relationally-situated objects rather than raw undifferentiated context in order to act safely and recoverably. This paper treats these three as structurally related instances of one pattern rather than as a single unified theory, and is explicit throughout about which claims are established, which are contested, and which remain the author’s own prior framework requiring further definition before public presentation. Keywords: interface theory of perception, attention and filtering, participatory universe, AI continuity, object-oriented cognition, philosophy of perception, foundations of physics, human-readable interfaces This is the fifth paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) and its companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) propose that bounded objects give AI runtimes operational grip on overwhelming context. Continuity, Authority, Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) proposes a control grammar for governing those objects, and Canonical Tokens (Gelhaus, 2026d) proposes a minimal- representation principle for a specific class of them. This paper steps back from AI- facing architecture specifically to ask a broader question those four papers assume but do not examine directly: is the filtering pattern they describe for AI runtimes a special case of something more general, observed independently in other domains that have nothing to do with artificial intelligence? This paper’s claim is bounded rather than triumphant: the pattern recurs; the recurrence is worth naming; the recurrence does not, by itself, prove any single grand unifying theory of consciousness, reality, or mind. 1. One Pattern, Three Domains The pattern under examination has a simple shape. An undifferentiated field exists, containing far more information than any single act of engagement with it can use. Something happens to that field - evolutionary tuning, an act of measurement, a design choice - that converts an unusable totality into a bounded, navigable, action- relevant structure. The structure that results is not the field itself. It is a rendering of the field, shaped by what the receiving system can use. This paper examines three instances of that shape: biological perception, a contested but serious position within physics regarding observation and reality, and AI-facing project continuity. The claim of this paper is not that these three instances share a hidden underlying mechanism in any strong metaphysical sense. The claim is narrower and more defensible: they share a recognizable structural pattern, and that recurrence is worth documenting carefully, with the boundaries of each domain’s evidence kept visible rather than blurred together. 2. Perceptual Filtering: The Interface Theory of Perception Human perception does not present reality as it is. This is not a controversial claim within perceptual science; it is close to a starting assumption. The interface theory of perception goes further, arguing that perception is actively shaped by evolutionary fitness rather than by accuracy: an organism whose perceptual system reported the true structure of reality, rather than a simplified, fitness-relevant rendering of it, would in general be outcompeted by an organism whose perceptual system reported only what mattered for survival and reproduction, formalized through evolutionary game-theoretic simulations comparing fitness-tuned versus truth-tuned perceptual strategies (Hoffman, Singh, and Prakash, 2015; Hoffman, 2019). The often-used analogy is a computer desktop: a blue rectangular icon is not blue, rectangular, or located where it appears in any deep physical sense, but the icon is not a lie either. It is a functional interface that lets a user interact correctly with underlying complexity the user does not need to perceive directly in order to act successfully. Perception, on this view, works the same way: it is not a window onto reality, but an interface to it, and the interface is good exactly because it hides almost everything that is not immediately useful. This paper uses Hoffman’s theory the same bounded way Artificial Tangibility already does (Gelhaus, 2026a): not as proof that reality is somehow less real than it appears, but as a rigorous, published source for the general claim that successful engagement with an overwhelming field often depends on filtering, not full access. 3. Attentional Filtering: Learned, Individual, and Tunable A separate and complementary body of work addresses a narrower question: even after perception has already reduced an overwhelming field to something perceivable, a further bottleneck exists at the level of attention. Donald Broadbent’s filter model of attention proposed that incoming information passes through an early selective filter before deeper processing, based on physical characteristics of the input rather than its meaning (Broadbent, 1958). Refinements of this model, particularly Anne Treisman’s attenuation theory, showed that the filter is not simply on or off for a given input channel; it can be tuned by prior relevance and learned salience, which is why a person’s own name reliably breaks through an otherwise fully ignored background conversation. This second filter is important for this paper’s argument because it is individually variable in a way perceptual interface theory, being a species-level claim, is not. Two people with the same perceptual apparatus can attend to entirely different features of the same field, because their attentional filter has been tuned differently by different histories. This paper treats this as the second layer of filtering: perception supplies a species-general interface; attention, shaped by lived experience, supplies an individually-tuned filter on top of it. 4. Observation and Reality: A Contested Position in Physics The most speculative domain examined in this paper is the foundations-of-physics literature on the role of observation in constituting physical reality. This section is written with more caution than Sections 2 and 3, because the claims here are genuinely contested within physics itself, not merely simplified for a general audience. John Archibald Wheeler, a major twentieth-century physicist who worked with Niels Bohr and coined the term black hole, proposed a position he called “It from Bit” and a related Participatory Anthropic Principle: that physical reality at its foundation may derive from binary distinctions registered through acts of observation, and that the universe may be best understood not as a fixed backdrop that observers happen to appear in, but as what Wheeler called a self-excited circuit, in which observer- participation is in some sense necessary to render the universe’s history definite (Wheeler, 1990). Wheeler’s own language was deliberately provocative: he proposed replacing the word “observer” with “participator,” and described reality as arising from “billions upon billions of acts of observer-participancy.” This paper does not adopt Wheeler’s position as established fact, and it would be a serious overclaim to present it that way. Wheeler’s ideas remain a minority, actively debated interpretive position regarding the foundations of quantum mechanics, not a consensus finding, and many physicists reject the strong reading in which consciousness itself is required to make reality determinate. What this paper draws from Wheeler is narrower and more defensible: a serious physicist, working from genuine physical puzzles about measurement and observation, arrived independently at a structural claim of the same shape examined in Sections 2 and 3 - that an undifferentiated or indeterminate field becomes definite, legible reality only through an act of engagement by something positioned to register it. Whether that structural claim is true at the level of fundamental physics is not something this paper can settle. That the same structural shape recurs, independently, in a serious physicist’s foundational work is itself the relevant fact for this paper’s argument. 5. The Fourth Instance: Objects as Filters in AI-Facing Continuity The companion papers in this sequence describe a fourth instance of the same structural pattern, this time in an entirely artificial and non-biological setting. An AI runtime, given an unstructured pile of files, chat history, and instructions, faces exactly the problem Sections 2 through 4 describe in other domains: an overwhelming field containing far more information than can be usefully acted on without some prior structuring. Artificial Tangibility’s proposed solution is filtering by another name. A bounded object - a source, a receipt, a Blackboard, a draft - is a fitness-tuned rendering of the underlying project state, shaped not by evolutionary pressure but by deliberate human design, for the specific purpose of letting a non-embodied runtime act correctly without needing the totality of the project’s raw history (Gelhaus, 2026a). Continuity, Authority, and Directive (Gelhaus, 2026c) function as the tuning parameters of that filter: what must survive, what governs, what is safe to act on now. Canonical Tokens (Gelhaus, 2026d) addresses the floor of that filtering process, arguing that some references are already at their minimal correct form and should not be re-expanded once filtered into an established shape. The claim of this section is precise: AI-facing object orientation is not merely inspired by, or loosely analogous to, biological and physical filtering. It is a fourth, deliberately engineered instance of the same general problem-solving shape - undifferentiated field, filter, bounded unit, navigable world - applied to a domain (AI runtime orientation) where the filter is built by explicit human design rather than by evolution or physical law. 6. Holographic Return: A Bridge Requiring the Author’s Own Definition This section names a bridge concept from the author’s own prior work, and it is handled differently than Sections 2 through 5, for an important reason: unlike Hoffman, Broadbent, Wheeler, or the companion AI-continuity papers, this concept does not yet have a stable, precise public definition, and this paper should not manufacture one on its behalf. Based on the author’s prior published work and this sequence’s own recurring themes, Holographic Return appears to name something like the following: a fragment, if it has been filtered correctly, can carry enough of the structure of a larger whole to permit a return to that whole without requiring the fragment to contain the whole’s total information. This would place Holographic Return as a claim about what a good filter preserves, not merely what it discards - a companion concern to Sections 2 through 5, which have focused mainly on what filtering removes. This paper deliberately stops short of stating this as a settled claim, because doing so would risk misrepresenting the author’s own framework with more precision than the author has yet given it in public form. The correct scholarly move, and the one this paper takes, is to flag this section explicitly as requiring the author’s direct definition and review before any public release of this paper, in the same way this sequence has flagged sensitive or under-specified material in its companion works. This section should be treated as a placeholder marking where the bridge belongs, not as a completed argument. 7. What This Paper Does Not Claim Given the domains this paper touches, its boundaries deserve explicit, repeated statement rather than a single disclaimer buried in an introduction. This paper does not claim that AI runtimes perceive, are conscious, or have subjective experience in any sense comparable to biological perception. The AI- continuity instance of the filtering pattern (Section 5) is an engineered structural analogue, not evidence of machine sentience. This paper does not claim that Wheeler’s participatory universe proposal is established physics. It is a genuine, serious, contested position, presented in Section 4 with that status made explicit, not as settled fact. This paper does not claim that the recurrence of one structural pattern across four domains proves any single underlying metaphysical theory - not conscious realism, not panpsychism, not a designed universe, not any specific theological position the author may hold elsewhere. Structural recurrence is evidence that a pattern is real and worth studying across domains. It is not proof that the domains share a literal common cause. This paper does not yet fully state Holographic Return as a defined public claim, for the reasons given in Section 6. 8. Why the Recurrence Still Matters, Even Bounded This Tightly A reasonable objection to this paper is that, once every strong claim has been bounded away, what remains is only a loose family resemblance between four unrelated fields, interesting as trivia but not as argument. This paper’s response is that the recurrence is more useful than that objection allows, for a specific, practical reason demonstrated directly by this paper’s own companion sequence. The AI-continuity instance of this pattern (Section 5) was not developed by importing perceptual or physical theory into AI design on purpose. It was developed independently, through direct engineering pressure - AI runtimes kept failing in a specific, nameable way, and object-oriented filtering was the practical fix that worked. Only afterward did the structural resemblance to Hoffman’s perceptual interface theory, Broadbent’s attentional filter, and Wheeler’s participatory universe become visible. That order of discovery matters. When a practical engineering fix, arrived at independently under real operational pressure, turns out to share its underlying shape with findings from perceptual science and foundational physics, the correct conclusion is not that one domain proves another. The correct conclusion is that the underlying problem - how a bounded system makes an overwhelming field usable - may be a genuinely general one, worth studying as its own subject, wherever it appears. 9. BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL | GELHAUS 2026 The most practical path forward preserves the existing source-authority machinery and introduces targeted extensions: precise refusal diagnostics, exact-field source routing, event candidates distinct from their documentary appearances, versioned correction relationships, and optional evidence-gated relation exploration. Those extensions admit concrete tests and provide McPhetridge with incremental opportunities to improve coverage without compromising the safeguards that already work. The OOCC development record supplies a related methodological lesson. V3 succeeded V2 through a documented history of tests, negative findings, and implementation changes. An external critique of one version must be dated and tested against that version’s actual evidence; conclusions cannot be inherited unchanged after revisions. Applying the same standards of chronology, source identity, and measurable outcome to both architectures turns comparative criticism into an engineering instrument rather than a contest of presentation or assertion. This is a working-state candidate, not the sole governing OOCC orientation. Private source custody retained; original ID withheld from public supplement. Appendix A. Acceptance tests for proposed extensions The acceptance suite should pin code revision, configuration, source bytes, field normalization, external-model settings and computational budgets before each run. Hidden questions must remain separate from development examples. BENJAMIN GELHAUS · 14 NOVEMBER 2026 | 15 BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL | GELHAUS 2026 1. No regression in source authority. Existing integrity, supersession, restricted-source, conflict and negative controls must retain their answer support and refusal decisions. 2. Improved diagnostic truthfulness. Unsupported question grammar, absent eligible source, known source conflict, insufficient evidence and index-exhaustion must be separately labeled. 3. Exact identifiers without false pruning. Exact field/quote routing must improve source location in held-out cases without dropping contradictory eligible passages; test zero, one and multiple matches. 4. Distinct event identities. Multiple appearances of one message remain distinguishable source occurrences; equal subject lines must not force identity; changed bodies must trigger review. 5. Time-scoped correction. A later partial correction changes only its specified claim while retaining the original statement, provenance and prior assessment. 6. Candidate inference remains a candidate. Missing intermediate evidence stops the proposed relation; exploratory outputs do not appear as deterministic supported answers. 7. Operational receipts remain independent. Stored, dispatched, delivered, read, acknowledged and completed are distinct outcomes; every transition requires the designated evidence. 8. Measure operator burden. Report human labeling and correction time, CPU time, memory, bytes scanned, source-count coverage and false-bridge rates alongside top-k retrieval. The decisive falsifier of the present capability-gap claim is an identifiable, independently examined MPLPB implementation that reconstructs these relationships from unprepared original source records , with credible source citations, useful recall, low false-positive rates and no degradation of its existing authority protections. A reciprocal evaluation of OOCC should use the same original-source access, version pins, blinded scoring and error metrics, while also measuring workflow benefits not shared by the two intended designs. An early critical claim about OOCC is falsified only by evidence attached to the correct date and technical mechanism, not by an unrelated later success. BENJAMIN GELHAUS

CAD Control Grammar Continuity Authority
CAD Control Grammar Continuity, Authority, Directive: A Plain-Language Control Grammar for AI Work Benjamin Gelhaus Independent Researcher Abstract Long-running AI-assisted work often fails not because the system lacks information, but because the runtime cannot reliably determine what must survive, what governs, and what action is safe now. This paper proposes Continuity, Authority, and Directive (CAD) as a plain-language control grammar for discontinuous AI collaboration. Continuity names what must carry across runtime breaks. Authority distinguishes source, draft, current, historical, blocked, promoted, and off-limits material. Directive constrains the next permissible action. Together, these three terms form a lightweight governance layer that can be attached to project objects, retrieval results, memory traces, receipts, drafts, and handoff notes. The paper argues that CAD is not merely prompt-level guidance. Prompting is the delivery surface; CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. It turns unstructured context extension into structured context extension by giving the runtime a minimal re-entry interface: the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, weight, and next safe action. Its testable value lies in improved re-entry, source/current distinction, reduced context burden, error diagnosis, safe action selection, and handoff quality. Keywords: AI continuity, human-AI interaction, AI governance, context engineering, runtime orientation, source authority, directive control, AI state management, structured context, recoverable handoff This paper is the third paper in a sequence on AI-facing project structure. Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) argues that non-embodied AI runtimes benefit from bounded objects that carry usable structure. A companion paper (Gelhaus, 2026b) situates that argument against existing AI state-management patterns, including retrieval-augmented generation, agent memory, and blackboard coordination. The present paper focuses on the control grammar those objects need. Its claim is not that three words can solve all AI governance problems. Its claim is that long-running AI work needs a simple, human-readable way to separate persistence, authority, and action. CAD is proposed as that minimal grammar. 1. The Problem: Fluency Without Governance A language model can sound aligned with a project while being wrong about the state of the project. It may summarize an old draft well. It may continue a rejected route fluently. It may identify a relevant source while misunderstanding whether that source governs the present task. It may produce useful language while crossing a boundary the human assumed was obvious. This failure is not merely a failure of intelligence or effort. It is a failure of governance. The runtime has access to language but not enough declared structure. It can infer meaning locally, yet still misread what must survive, what counts as source, and what action is permitted now. Long-running AI-assisted work therefore needs more than better prompts, more memory, or larger context windows. It needs a control grammar: a small set of durable questions that can travel with the work and constrain how a runtime re- enters it. Continuity, Authority, and Directive are proposed as such a grammar. Each term names a different runtime risk. Continuity protects against loss. Authority protects against confusion. Directive protects against overreach. 2. Context Without Schema A common response to runtime drift is to provide more context. The user may paste more history, attach more files, summarize more background, or ask the model to consider everything. This often helps, but only when the added material is already shaped. Without declared structure, extended context can arrive as an undifferentiated context cloud. The runtime must infer, during generation, which parts are source, which are draft, which are stale, which are private, which are governing, which are background, and which action is allowed. The model is then forced to interpret the task and invent the schema of the workspace at the same time. CAD reverses that burden. It presents context as a structured interface before generation begins. Instead of asking the runtime to sort a pile of language, CAD declares the relevant objects, their authority states, their boundaries, their relations, their weights, and their next safe actions. This is not a stylistic improvement. It is a change in load pattern. The runtime is no longer asked to discover the project map from raw text. It receives the map first. 3. Why Continuity Alone Is Not Enough Continuity asks: what must survive the runtime? In discontinuous AI work, the runtime is not the durable carrier of the project. A session can end, a context window can fill, a tool can fail, a model can change, or a different runtime can enter later. If the project depends on the runtime remembering what happened, the project remains fragile. Continuity externalizes what must carry forward. It preserves active objects, governing sources, unresolved blockers, decisions, open questions, receipts, and next actions. It turns memory from a private session property into a project property. But continuity by itself is not enough. Preserving everything can preserve confusion. A project may contain old drafts, rejected ideas, repaired mistakes, private notes, public claims, speculative language, and current source material. If all of that survives without hierarchy, the next runtime has continuity but no governance. This is why the first term must be paired with the second. Continuity says what survives. Authority says what governs. 4. Authority as the Anti-Confusion Layer Authority asks: what counts as source, current, draft, historical, blocked, promoted, or off-limits? Authority is the anti-confusion layer of AI work. Without it, the runtime may treat polished text as governing simply because it is polished. It may treat repeated language as truth because it appears in several places. It may treat a retrieved document as current because retrieval made it visible. It may treat a completed draft as a public claim because the draft sounds complete. Authority separates existence from permission. A file may exist without governing. A receipt may prove that something happened without making it canonical. A draft may be valuable without being promoted. A source may govern one task but not another. A private constraint may shape reasoning without becoming public language. Authority also protects the human from the re-entry burden. Instead of re-explaining every hierarchy at the start of each session, the project can declare authority states in the objects themselves: current source, historical source, active draft, parked seed, blocked claim, internal note, promoted artifact, or public release. A runtime that knows authority can be corrected more precisely. The human no longer has to say, “That is wrong” in a general way. The human can say: you treated a draft as source, you treated a parked object as active, you promoted without authority, or you used a historical object as current. 5. Directive as the Anti-Overreach Layer Directive asks: what is the next safe action? Even when continuity and authority are clear, a runtime can still act too broadly. It may understand the project and still make an unauthorized move. It may summarize when it should verify, rewrite when it should append, merge when it should compare, publish when it should wait, or continue when access failure requires a stop. Directive reduces the action space. It turns general project understanding into a bounded next move: read first, compare only, summarize the active source, append a receipt, draft the next section, verify authority, stop if access fails, wait for human review, or do not touch this object. The directive is not merely a task instruction. It is a governance device. It tells the runtime how far its permission extends in the present moment. This matters because language models are optimized to continue. In many situations, continuation is useful. In governed work, unbounded continuation can be dangerous. Directive interrupts that momentum and replaces it with accountable movement. 6. CAD as a Minimal Runtime Governance Grammar Continuity, Authority, and Directive work together because they answer three different questions that a discontinuous runtime cannot safely infer on its own. Continuity: what must survive? Authority: what governs? Directive: what is safe now? These questions are deliberately plain. They do not require the runtime to import a complex theory before acting. They can be placed in project notes, handoff files, retrieval metadata, state boards, receipts, source maps, task tickets, or prompt templates. The point is not the format. The point is the separation of functions. When the three functions collapse into one instruction, errors become harder to diagnose. For example, a note that says “continue the paper” may hide multiple assumptions: which version of the paper, under what authority, with what boundaries, using what source, and toward what next action? CAD forces those assumptions into visible fields. The grammar can be attached to any AI-facing object. A source document can declare its continuity role, authority status, and permitted next actions. A draft can declare that it is active but not promoted. A receipt can declare what changed and what should happen next. A retrieval result can be treated as relevant but not governing until authority is checked. 7. Prompt Surface and Control Structure CAD should not be reduced to prompt engineering. Prompting is the visible delivery surface, but CAD is the structured policy layer carried through that surface. The runtime receives natural language, but the operative content is a governance model. A one-off prompt says: do this task. CAD says: this object exists, this object has this status, this source governs, this boundary cannot be crossed, this operation is allowed, this operation is forbidden, and this is the next safe move. In this sense, CAD functions less like ordinary prompting and more like a lightweight policy language for AI-assisted work. It combines the routing logic of directory services, the constraint logic of policy systems, and the accessibility of natural language. Its purpose is to tell a discontinuous runtime what object exists, what authority it carries, where it belongs, and what operation is safe now. The analogy to programming language is bounded but useful. CAD is not a programming language in the conventional compiler or runtime sense. It is a language layer for governing AI work. Like mature programming languages, it expands beyond isolated commands into objects, permissions, scope, state, authority, allowed operations, blocked operations, and error handling. The prompt is therefore not the architecture. The prompt is the carrier. The structure hidden behind the words is what makes the system work. 8. Structuralized Context Extension CAD also changes how extended context is loaded. In many workflows, context extension means placing more history into the runtime’s active window. This can increase available information while also increasing ambiguity, distraction, and stale- state risk. CAD turns context extension into structured context extension. The runtime does not need to reload the whole project. It needs the current object map, authority state, boundary conditions, object weight, and next safe action. This reduces re-entry cost. A future runtime can enter through a minimal interface rather than through an entire unfiltered archive. The active structure points to the materials that matter now and explains how they should be treated. This claim should be evaluated as an operational mechanism rather than a universal benchmark. In practice, structuralized context can allow large, multi-document, multi-runtime projects to remain workable because the system does not ask each runtime to ingest the whole history again. It asks the runtime to load the interface to the project state. The result is a smaller and cleaner context hit: not less project knowledge, but less unstructured project burden. 9. Failure Modes: Lost, Confused, and Mishandled Objects The CAD grammar provides a useful error taxonomy. Without continuity, the runtime loses the object. The work may have happened, but the next session cannot recover it. The human has to reconstruct the room from memory. Without authority, the runtime confuses the object. It may find the object but misunderstand its status. It may treat draft as source, old as current, private as public, parked as active, or rejected as live. Without directive, the runtime mishandles the object. It may understand what the object is and still act beyond permission. It may rewrite when it should read, publish when it should wait, or mutate a source when it should preserve it. This taxonomy makes failure more repairable. Instead of treating AI drift as a vague malfunction, the system can ask: was this a continuity error, an authority error, or a directive error? That question turns confusion into telemetry. 10. Relationship to Prompting, Memory, Retrieval, and Tool Use CAD does not replace prompting. It gives prompting structure. A prompt no longer has to carry the whole project if the objects around the prompt carry continuity, authority, and directive. CAD does not replace memory. It governs what memory means. A remembered or retrieved item may still need an authority state before the runtime acts on it. CAD does not replace retrieval. It controls how retrieved material is handled. Retrieval can surface a candidate object; CAD helps determine whether that object governs, informs, warns, or remains background. CAD does not replace tool use or agent loops. It constrains them. A tool-using agent still needs to know whether the current action is allowed, whether the source can be modified, and whether the next move requires human review. CAD does not replace human-in-the-loop design. It clarifies where the human must remain authoritative. It gives the runtime a visible reason to stop, wait, verify, or ask for review rather than silently converting uncertainty into action. 11. CAD and Artificial Tangibility Artificial Tangibility (Gelhaus, 2026a) names the way bounded objects give non- embodied runtimes operational grip. CAD supplies the governance grammar for those objects. An object without CAD may be named but under-specified. The runtime may know that the object exists without knowing whether it must survive, whether it governs, or what action is safe next. CAD turns the object from a handle into a governable unit of work. The relationship can be stated simply: Artificial Tangibility gives the runtime something to hold. CAD tells the runtime how that object must be preserved, trusted, and acted upon. This is especially important in high-context work involving drafts, sources, private boundaries, public claims, multiple tools, or long handoffs. In such work, the difference between an object and a governed object is the difference between local coherence and recoverable project movement. 12. Evaluation Criteria CAD should be evaluated operationally. It should not be accepted merely because the vocabulary is useful. The first criterion is re-entry quality. A future runtime should enter a project faster and with less human reconstruction when continuity objects are explicit. The second criterion is source-current distinction. The runtime should make fewer errors that come from treating old, draft, or background material as current authority. The third criterion is context burden. The runtime should require less raw history when the project provides a structuralized re-entry interface. The fourth criterion is safe action selection. The runtime should choose narrower and more appropriate actions when directives are explicit. The fifth criterion is error catchability. When the runtime fails, the failure should be easier to classify as continuity, authority, directive, schema, or boundary error. The sixth criterion is handoff quality. A CAD-governed handoff should tell the next runtime what survived, what governs, what is blocked, and what action is safe now. The seventh criterion is human burden. CAD should reduce the amount of repeated explanation required from the human at each new session. These criteria make the paper’s claim testable. If CAD does not improve re-entry, authority distinction, context burden, safe action, error diagnosis, or handoff quality, the grammar should be revised. 13. Boundary Conditions and Limits CAD is not a complete safety system. It does not guarantee factual correctness, prevent all hallucination, enforce access control by itself, or replace formal security infrastructure. It is a governance grammar, not a total architecture. CAD also depends on disciplined use. If continuity objects are stale, authority labels are inaccurate, directives are vague, or the structural interface is not maintained, the grammar can reproduce confusion rather than solve it. The method is most useful where project state matters across sessions: research, writing, analysis, software planning, multi-document review, claim-sensitive work, or human-AI collaboration across multiple tools. For simple one-off tasks, CAD may be unnecessary. A casual rewrite or single-turn question does not require a full continuity grammar. The method matters most when the cost of drift, stale context, or unauthorized action is high. 14. Conclusion Continuity, Authority, and Directive form a minimal control grammar for long- running AI-assisted work. Continuity preserves what must survive. Authority declares what governs. Directive constrains what action is safe now. The grammar is useful because it separates failures that otherwise blur together. A runtime can lose the object, confuse the object, mishandle the object, or drown inside unstructured context. CAD makes those failures nameable and therefore more repairable. The broader significance is practical. AI runtimes do not need to be treated as continuous selves in order to participate in complex work. They need project environments that externalize continuity, declare authority, constrain action, and structuralize context before generation begins. The final claim is modest but operational: long-running AI collaboration improves when humans do not merely give models more context, but give them governed objects - objects that say what must survive, what governs, what is safe now, and how the runtime can re-enter without carrying the entire archive. BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL
BEYOND GUARDED RETRIEVAL | GELHAUS 2026 The most practical path forward preserves the existing source-authority machinery and introduces targeted extensions: precise refusal diagnostics, exact-field source routing, event candidates distinct from their documentary appearances, versioned correction relationships, and optional evidence-gated relation exploration. Those extensions admit concrete tests and provide McPhetridge with incremental opportunities to improve coverage without compromising the safeguards that already work. The OOCC development record supplies a related methodological lesson. V3 succeeded V2 through a documented history of tests, negative findings, and implementation changes. An external critique of one version must be dated and tested against that version’s actual evidence; conclusions cannot be inherited unchanged after revisions. Applying the same standards of chronology, source identity, and measurable outcome to both architectures turns comparative criticism into an engineering instrument rather than a contest of presentation or assertion.
